item.title: Launching the Global Priorities Research Group at LSE - currently hiring for two 4-year postdocs
item.description:
Published on October 22, 2026 3:41 PM GMT

I'm very happy to announce the launch of the Global Priorities Research Group, a new research group at LSE dedicated to the study of ethical prioritisation. We are hosted by LSE’s Centre for Philosophy of Natural and Social Science (CPNSS) and aim to pursue philosophical research designed to help individuals and institutions decide how they should allocate scarce resources to realise the best outcomes for humanity and the wider world, continuing the work of Oxford’s Global Priorities Institute.

GPRG aims to put particular emphasis on philosophical research that helps us navigate the largest-scale challenges associated with the impacts of transformative AI. We'll also consider how to compare and weight the interests of different kinds of minds - be they human, animal, or artificial - as well as foundational questions related to value and rational choice with the potential to reorient our priorities across a wide range of issues. You can find out more about our research programme here.

I'm leading the group, and I’m joined at LSE by Teruji Thomas. We're currently hiring for two 4-year postdoctoral researchers, so if you'd be interested in joining the group, please consider making an application before the deadline on November 15th.

item.title: CEA is now independent of Effective Ventures
item.description:
Published on October 23, 2026 12:38 PM GMT

Hi everyone! I’m CEA’s new Chief of Staff. I also serve as our Board Liaison, and I’m posting to introduce you to CEA’s new independent board. I’m happy to be a point of contact for any questions you have about them, or the recruiting process we ran to find and select them!

TL;DR: As of October 1, 2026, CEA is an independent organization, with our first independent board. 

Why we spun out

When we announced our spinout in 2024, we said that bringing our operations in-house and setting up our own legal entities would help us pursue our mission better. EV is winding down, and we wanted governance and operations built for what CEA is today. That’s now in place: our own operations team, our own entities, and a board accountable to CEA specifically.

Meet our new board

Stien van der Ploeg (Board Chair) is the executive director of Animal Charity Evaluators. Before joining ACE, Stien worked 20 years supporting various causes in multiple countries. They now use their leadership, strategy, and philanthropy skills to help more people help more animals.

Jacob Eliosoff is a computer programmer from Montreal who lives in NYC. He started out in tech startups and has since worked in finance, crypto, and long ago as a teacher. He’s been involved in many projects related to effective altruism, including being on the boards of EA NYC, The Humane League, and Collider.nyc (an AI safety/impact coworking hub).

Andrés Jiménez Zorrilla is a former private equity professional turned entrepreneur (both for- and not-for-profit). He is an active member of the EA community, the co-founder and former CEO of Shrimp Welfare Project, and a trustee of Ambitious Impact. He is currently working on navigating the transition to a world with artificial super intelligence. 

 

Each of these three combines values alignment with board experience and impressive results in their own field. The search was a lot like an executive search, but where we needed three leaders instead of one. We weren’t sure we could find even one person who matched the spec we wrote, so finding three was far from a given. We started with 250+ referrals and ended up with our top choices, all of them busy people with plenty of other options for how they spend their time. We take their decision to commit significant personal time to CEA as a vote of confidence in our mission and future direction.

For this first board we prioritized independence, board experience, and experience outside EA, and the new board is planning a second round of recruitment in 2027 to expand membership and round out their skill sets to provide effective oversight to CEA. 

What changes

Honestly, not much for our day-to-day work. Our teams, managers, and strategic direction are largely the same! 

What does change is how CEA operates. Under EV’s structure, the legal separation between the US and UK entities made it hard to run a single organization (for example, our UK-based COO couldn’t make certain decisions for the US side, and our US-based CEO couldn’t make them for the UK side). Now that CEA has its own entities and its own Operations Team, the people accountable for CEA’s work can make the decisions that affect it, and we can build on what we learned in the EV era, including stronger compliance across the organization. 

The spinout was largely (and intentionally) a boring operational process, but it matters to us. It removed administrative hurdles that took up time and attention, and it lets us focus on our mission.

Thank you

This was a major operational undertaking. We’re very grateful to the staff and board members at CEA and EV, past and present, whose work made it possible, alongside everything else they do.

item.title: We tested 14 meat-reduction messages with real money at stake. Celebrities and history did best.
item.description:
Published on October 26, 2026 10:41 AM GMT

TL;DR

  • In an online experiment with 4,761 Americans, short presentations built from 14 message modules increased the relative value people placed on a plant-based gift basket by $10.05, about 26% of its original value, compared with a placebo video.
  • Content mattered much more than quantity. Describing celebrities' plant-based diets and framing meat reduction as being on the right side of history produced the largest gains.
  • More modules, captive viewing, and asking people to eliminate meat (rather than reduce it) made no significant difference.
  • This is a real-stakes choice, which is better than stated intentions, but it is a single choice measured immediately after exposure. It says nothing about what people ate the following week.

Why I'm posting this now

There has been a lot of discussion lately about whether EA has given up on diet change. Seth Ariel Green argues it hasn't: funders deprioritised it because the evidence was weak, and they would back new approaches that come with better evidence. He also asked more of us to post rather than polish.

Here's my quick contribution! Note, the meta-analysis by Green, Mathur and colleagues found that meaningfully reducing meat consumption remains an unsolved problem, and a single online experiment does not change that. However, it does offer a direct comparison of many message types against the same real-stakes outcome, which the literature mostly lacks.

What we did

With Jacy Anthis and Joshua Tasoff, I ran a large online experiment with 4,761 Americans, recruited through Prolific in September 2023.

  • Treatment: each participant in the treatment group saw a presentation of either 5 or 9 modules, drawn at random from 14. (Full scripts and videos are on OSF.) Each module was one to two minutes of narrated slides. Half of the participants were required to watch the full presentation, while the other half had the ability to skip modules. The 14 modules were:
    • Identity (being on the right side of history)
    • Animal suffering
    • An animal rescue story
    • Environment
    • Pandemic risk
    • Blaming the industry rather than consumers
    • Health
    • Whether individual choices make a difference
    • Celebrities
    • Plant-based eating as a growing trend
    • Convenience
    • Nutrition tips
    • Willpower
    • New food technology
  • Control: a placebo video.
  • Outcome: real-stakes willingness to pay for a meat-based versus a plant-based gift basket, measured before and after exposure. Both baskets had a $100 retail value. For each, people chose between the basket and a cash bonus rising from $0 to $100 in $5 steps, and we told them 20 participants would be picked at random to have one of their choices carried out for real, receiving either the cash or the basket.

Because modules were combined at random, we could estimate the effect of each module, as well as features such as the number of modules, whether captive vs free audiences, and whether the closing ask was to reduce or to eliminate meat. The study was pre-registered and funded by the Food Systems Research Fund and the Sentience Institute. One secondary outcome asked people how much of a possible bonus they would donate to ProVeg. (However, we ran the study in 2023, before I joined ProVeg, and this is my own academic work rather than ProVeg's).

What we found

On average, the treatment increased the relative valuation of the plant-based basket by $10.05 compared with the control group, about 26% of its original value.

The effects varied widely by content:

  • Largest gains: describing celebrities' plant-based diets, and framing meat reduction as being on the right side of history. The identity module added $3.61 to the plant-meat gap (95% CI 1.79 to 5.43), and celebrities $3.27 (1.45 to 5.09). Industry ($2.51) and animal suffering ($2.30) were the only other modules that were significant on their own.
  • No significant effect: adding more modules, captive viewing, and asking people to eliminate rather than reduce meat.
  • Weakest: the growing-trend ($0.24) and pandemic ($0.29) modules. Every module's estimate was positive, so nothing backfired.

The two strongest modules have something in common. One shows people others admire already eating this way, and the other asks how future generations will judge us. Neither gives new facts about meat. The next two strongest, blaming the industry and showing animal suffering, are standard advocacy content, though. Most differences between modules aren't statistically significant.

People who already wanted to cut down on meat (24% of the sample) moved the most: their effect was $5.35 larger. Effects were also larger for women (by $3.53) and for people over 45 (by $3.80). 

What this can and can't tell us

What it can: the outcome is a choice with money at stake, which is a step up from stated intentions. Randomising modules lets us compare message types against each other on the same outcome, instead of testing one campaign against nothing.

What it can't:

  • Persistence. The choice was made straight after the presentation, in the same session. We don't know whether anyone ate differently afterwards.
  • One product, one decision. Valuing a gift basket is narrower than changing a diet.
  • Setting. An online US sample, paid to take part, watching a presentation they were asked to watch. Real-world reach and attention will be lower. Even when people could skip modules, they skipped only about 14% of them, so we learnt little about captive versus skippable viewing.

So I'd read this as evidence about which messages are worth taking into a field trial, rather than evidence that messaging reduces meat consumption.

item.title: Discrimination in AI safety: A call for incident reports
item.description:
Published on October 25, 2026 5:08 PM GMT

TL;DR 

We (Frances, Sarah, and Geetha) work in AI safety and the broader EA ecosystem. We are increasingly concerned about sexual harassment, workplace harassment, and discrimination in these spaces. Through our advocacy, we have heard numerous firsthand accounts of ineffective or nonexistent reporting systems and anti-harassment policies, dismissive organisational attitudes, and harassment incidents being mishandled. We are now collecting incident reports through confidential calls, so we can make the case to funders and organisations for minimum standards on how harassment is prevented and handled. If you have an experience to share, we’d love to hear from you (please fill out this form).[1]

How you can help

Please share this widely: within your organisation, in relevant Slack and fellowship groups, on social media, directly with people you know, and anywhere else you’re comfortable.

Our ultimate goal

We will produce a list of recommendations for how organisations in the space can improve, including policies, guidance on handling conflicts of interest in complaints, resources to support victims through reporting, and standards for reporting and codes of conduct at events and co-working spaces.

To make these recommendations effective, we need to understand the issues victims are facing and be able to explain the scope of the problem. We believe a collection of concrete incidents is an important first step.

We plan to advocate for better baseline standards across organisations in the ecosystem by approaching funders such as Coefficient Giving, Longview Philanthropy, FLF, and SFF, and urging them to require minimum standards from their grantees. (Note: we do not have full details on each funder’s existing standards, but have been disappointed by what we do know.) We are also planning to draft an open letter to organisations in the space that professionals will have the chance to sign.

We are doing this independently. We are not funded by anyone, and this project is not affiliated with any organisation, including our employers.

Our ask 

We’re asking people to share incidents of sexual harassment, workplace harassment, and discrimination with us. Right now, we’re particularly focussed on AI safety, but we’re also keen to hear about incidents within effective altruism more broadly. These can be firsthand accounts (something you experienced directly) or corroborated secondhand accounts (something you directly witnessed, or an incident you have evidence of). If you’re not sure whether something “counts,” please speak with us anyway. We’d love to hear from as many people as possible.

How it works, plus confidentiality & anonymity 

We’ll ask you to have a call with one of us to record the incident. Nothing you share will go further without your permission. We’ll work with you to decide what, if anything, we can share and how widely (e.g. you might be comfortable with it being shared within the ecosystem but not in a public post, or with naming an organisation but not yourself). You can change your mind at any time. The only exception is if you disclose an imminent threat to someone’s safety (e.g. “I have heard that [Name 1] plans to do [violent thing] to [Name 2]”), in which case we would notify [Name 2].

You’ll need to identify yourself to the person you speak with, so we can confirm that every report comes from a verified source. You can ask for your details to stay anonymous to the other two of us.

(General note: If you’ve previously disclosed an incident to any of us, it will not be included in this project in any capacity by default. If you would like it included, please reach out again and let one of us know.)

(Second general note: At least one other person will help us analyse and write up our findings. Anyone helping at that stage will only have access to information we’ve been given explicit permission to share.)

Who should you talk to? 

Any of us! Or all of us. It’s totally up to you. We know you may not feel comfortable talking to any of the three of us, so capacity permitting, we’ll try to offer one or two other people you could speak with later on.

Who we are and how to contact us

Please fill out this form with, at minimum, your name and email. If applicable, you can specify who you’d like to talk to. Once you submit, we’ll reach out to book a 30-minute call. The only people with access to form submissions are Sarah, Geetha, and Frances. To quickly reiterate, we are working on this project in a personal capacity and not in affiliation with our employers. All views expressed are our own.

Sarah Gokhale
Hello! I am the Events Lead at Coefficient Giving. Previously, I was a Recruiter also at Coefficient Giving and before that I was on the AI Events and EAG teams at the Centre for Effective Altruism. I left CEA because of how badly the org and its leaders mishandled Frances’s sexual harassment investigation. I gave a critical exit interview about this that was never escalated to leadership.

I got into effective altruism while doing a PhD in moral philosophy at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York City.

I moved to the Bay Area in August 2026 from Portland, Oregon. Since then, I have been motivated to speak increasingly publicly about the sexual harassment and discrimination I witness in the AI safety field on a weekly basis. I am eager to speak candidly with and be a resource to anyone who would find it useful.

Geetha 
Hello :) I’m a PhD student at UC Berkeley working on biosecurity, specifically transmission suppression / indoor air quality interventions. I’ve been vegan since I was 14, and I learned about effective altruism in my second year of undergrad. After that, I began exploring global health and animal welfare work, and later transitioned into biosecurity. Before my PhD, I completed my Master’s in the Sculpting Evolution Group at MIT under Dr. Kevin Esvelt, and I’ve also worked at SecureBio.

Over my 8 years in the community, I’ve grown increasingly concerned about incidents of harassment and discrimination, and about attitudes towards them. I supported Frances throughout reporting sexual harassment to CEA, including attending calls alongside her. I was shocked by how much self-advocacy it took to get any help and by how visibly uncomfortable and inexperienced senior leaders were throughout the process. The stories I have heard from members in the community since this incident have been equally as concerning. 

Frances
Hi! I'm Frances, and I'm a Project Manager for Events at FAR.AI. Before that, I worked on the EA Global team at the Centre for Effective Altruism, and before that, I was an Operations Associate at AI Safety Support. 

I've previously written about the sexual harassment I experienced at the Centre for Effective Altruism, which was mishandled and ultimately ended in a settlement. While I am by no means an expert, I have firsthand experience navigating reporting systems and understand how terrible it can be.

Through this project, I want to give victims a chance to share their experiences without having to put themselves in a stressful or unsafe position. More than anything, I care about victims and want to support however I can. I also believe AI risk is an incredibly important problem, and the field desperately needs talent. For people to do their best work, they need to be able to work safely. I want our professional ecosystem to be as healthy and functional as possible.

    I posted a different form link on X. I am still checking that one, but we're planning to predominantly use this new form link moving forward. I am the only one with access to previous form responses, and as stated, those will not be shared with anyone else.

item.title: Small Groups of Correlated Researchers
item.description:
Published on October 26, 2026 7:03 PM GMT

Summary: The actions taken this decade may be exceptionally important for the future of civilization, but we should be unusually hesitant to proclaim that any course of action is “best.” Still, we should try to think carefully about how we'll influence the future.

This post was written as part of an introduction to a new reading group I’m starting called “Doing Good in the Age of AGI.” If you want to follow along, the full curriculum can be found here.

Uncertain in the best of times

Do you think freezing rent prices would be good for the economic middle class? How confident are you? 

You might have an answer that you like, but you’re probably not that confident in it. Perhaps you haven’t formally studied economics, but maybe you’ve had some passing interest in the topic. Ever since Mamdani’s mayoral campaign became a talking point across the country, or since his rent freeze passed in June of 2026, discussion of this economic policy has shifted back into the public spotlight. Maybe you’ve tried to read the arguments on both sides, and you’ve noticed that there’s a lot to read. As it turns out, people are opinionated enough that 82% of renters and homebuyers believe there should be caps on rent increases, but a survey of the top economists shows that only 2%[1] think that rent caps would make the middle class substantially better off over the course of a decade (with some of the disagreement coming from whether or not a benefit would be “substantial”). And within this gap between public sentiment and expert opinion, there is so much discourse and research. The American Economics Association has 23,000 members, about half of which are academics, and a single meta-analysis on rent control reviews over 200 papers. 

A lot of thinking has gone into finding the truth about this specific question. You might believe that this puts you in a good position to make claims about the effects of rent control. But even if you think expert consensus is pretty unified and easy to defer to, you might fail to explain why, exactly, the occasional dissenter may be wrong or misleading. It’s reasonable for a layperson to feel somewhat uncertain about the efficacy of rent controls, but they can still look toward the thousands of hours of collective thought that have gone into studying this topic to get some answer. The same is also roughly true for the field of climate science, which published over 15,000 peer-reviewed studies in 2025, and political science, which has thousands of full-time researchers.

I bring up rent control because it’s small and specific, has a pretty clear expert consensus, a wide body of evidence to refer to, and yet still remains a large source of public disagreement and uncertainty. 

Now, imagine trying to answer a question that has none of those qualities. A question like, “How can we do the most good?”

No question may be more important than, “What is the most important problem for us to work on?” Despite this, it receives much less attention globally than the content of an introductory economics class. In 2025, GiveWell had about 40 full-time employees trying to answer the question, “What is the most cost-effective way to save a life, given the best evidence we have?” That same year, Animal Charity Evaluators had about 12 FTEs trying to figure out which animal welfare strategies will actually help animals, and as of October 2026, Coefficient Giving has 55 people on their Global Catastrophic Risks team (although not all of them are directly doing prioritization work). In 2025, Rethink Priorities estimated that there were only about 20 total FTEs in the world trying to determine the most important cause to work on, and only 4 FTEs trying to compare the cost-effectiveness of interventions across different causes.[2] And only a fraction of these employees are trying to answer this question by considering the possibility of truly transformative AI. 

If you look ahead at the curriculum’s future weeks, you may notice that Forethought (an organization with close to 16 FTEs) has contributed about 9 of our required readings and 3 of our additional recommendations.[3] Aside from the number of researchers being small, they’re also highly correlated in the sense that many of them hold similar assumptions, many of which could turn out to be false. In the entire curriculum, there are only four readings I’m not confident are written by effective altruists.[4] Their authors are Eliezer Yudkowsky (the primary founder of the rationalist movement), Jason Hausenloy (who I feel less confident about being an EA because he works at CAIS), the Forecasting Research Institute (which receives funding from Coefficient Giving), and something called “The Greater Good Magazine.” A relatively small cultural lineage is producing the vast majority of our understanding about this topic.  

There’s a strong, mathematical reason to be deathly afraid of these correlations, and it has to do with our ability to get rid of the Optimizer’s Curse. The curse works something like this: imagine you’re trying to figure out which cause area (out of 30 or so) is the most important. When you make an impact evaluation for each cause, your estimate will include both the size of a cause’s true impact and the size of any mistakes you made in your assessment. As a result, when you try to choose the most important cause area, you’ll probably choose something that you’ve significantly overestimated the importance of by making a mistake. 

Graph showing the Optimizer’s Curse. We only see our estimation of the impact, rather than the actual impact, which causes us to ignore the best cause in favor of a cause whose impact we overestimated. 

And, when you’re extra uncertain about something (such as what the future will look like, or what threat has the highest chance of causing extinction), the size of the curse is amplified.[5] If we have a diverse pool of researchers evaluating causes independently, this can significantly reduce how much we overestimate the top cause. But if the researchers are correlated and share the same mistakes, no number of separate researchers will be able to get rid of the curse completely. 

Graph: Using Titotal’s Optimizer’s Curse model for existential risks, I simulated 10,000 instances of 500 different researchers evaluating the danger of different causes, aggregating their results, and estimating the impact of working on the top one. Different r values correspond to different levels of correlated mistakes. When their mistakes are completely uncorrelated (r = 0), aggregating research results leads to no Optimizer’s Curse most of the time, while researchers who share many of the same mistakes (high r value) significantly overestimate the size of the top threat most of the time. 

When writing this curriculum, I did my best to include readings from a good number of perspectives, but in practice, so few people are taking time to think seriously about what transformative AI could do to the future and how we can best prepare for it. If we’re going to get AGI or ASI by 2040, then most of our best guesses for how to make the future good are currently coming from small groups of highly correlated researchers. This should make us terrified.

Moving Forward

There’s a lot of work to be done and a lot of wrong ways to do it, but we still may have good reasons to be optimistic about our room for progress. 

Our understanding of transformative AI cause prioritization is limited enough that someone smart can say valuable things within a few months of thinking about these problems. It’s small enough that I felt comfortable making this reading group six weeks long, instead of eight. If you set aside the time to do some research, talk to some experts, and perhaps do a “minimal trust investigation”, you can make helpful critiques that sharpen our models of the world. Even if your arguments miss important context or internal research, the broader community still benefits from the information you share. At the end of the day, Forethought is just a bunch of smart people who have taken time to think about highly neglected fields. It wouldn’t take a newcomer especially long to make similarly helpful contributions.[6]

But while novel work can help, there are wrong ways to adjust for a lack of differing perspectives. We reduce the overestimations caused by Optimizer’s Curse by correcting our mistaken beliefs, and not every challenge is a correction. Taking on diverse views simply for the sake of getting different answers does not necessarily bring us closer to the truth, the same way that the best forecasters will not make better predictions by averaging their predictions with worse predictions. If you disagree with someone about something, figure out what evidence has led them to believe something different than you, and see if you can reconcile this gap.

But even though the groups thinking seriously about these problems are pretty small, I feel hopeful about the EA community’s ability to make some good judgments. They respond well to criticism, challenge each other’s assumptions, and are keen to build more accurate models of the world. The EA community also disproportionately produces superforecasters and supports tons of forecasting research because they earnestly try to improve at this. When I was writing this post, I tried to make a list of mistakes that the AI safety community had historically made, that should have been obvious to avoid. Most examples[7] I found were contested, hard to predict, and were quickly pivoted away from when shown to be false. For the most part, our models of the future are limited because of a lack of time and resources, not because of a lack of care on behalf of the people making them.[8]

At the end of the day, though, our understanding of the future is limited. If we try to prepare for any specific vision of it, we will certainly make mistakes, and there’s a large chance our work could be trivial or net-negative. Despite this, I think that trying our best to improve the lives of the many future generations of humans, animals, and other sentient creatures yet to come is one of the most important things we can do.

item.title: Doing Good in the Age of AGI: Recommended Reading List
item.description:
Published on October 26, 2026 11:31 PM GMT

Tl;dr: This is my recommended curriculum for a 6-week "Doing Good in the Age of AGI" reading group. It is primarily focused on cause prioritization in recent months, and it is intended for an audience that has already completed an EA intro fellowship or has a similar amount of context. 

While creating this reading list, I tried my best to ensure that all the required readings were enjoyable, information-dense, and discussable. For the most part, I also tried to remove duplicate content. This is less true for the optional readings, but there's still a lot of great stuff there. It turns out that the EA community is pretty fantastic and flush with ideas! Still, if anyone has thoughts about serious oversights in this list or ways to improve it while keeping the required readings below 1 hour per week, I'd love to hear it. 

There is also a version of this doc with prettier formatting.

What is this?

Effective Altruism has long sought to answer the question, “How do I do the most good with the resources available to me?” From this question, it has trended toward several patterns of thinking, as it has found those styles to be most helpful for answering these questions:

  • Comparing differences in impact: The most cost-effective interventions are often vastly more impactful than the median ones, and time spent prioritizing between areas can lead to actions that do vastly more good than others
  • Recognizing triage: Any hour that we spend working on one project is necessarily not spent dedicated to another project, and any amount of money donated to one charity is necessarily not given to another. We’re constantly choosing not to support a variety of important interventions and causes, and we should consider that sacrifice as we decide what is worth working on. 
  • Recognizing the differences between “fuzzies” and “utilons”: Interventions that may intuitively appeal to us might (“fuzzies”) not be the ones that help the most (“utilons”), or that really treat others with the dignity of equality.
  • The Scout Mindset: Rather than seek to defend positions that we already hold, like a soldier defending their territory, we should try to create an accurate map of reality that helps us make better decisions. 
  • Thinking at the margin: When we ask ourselves the question, “What ought we to do?”, we are not asking the question, “What should everyone in the world do?”. Our decisions should be informed by our particular circumstances and the full effects of our decisions alone. For example, at the current margin, an additional cancer researcher does not make very much progress toward curing cancer, while a single person working on early detection for deadly pandemics could be responsible for breakthroughs that the field’s limited resources haven’t had time to explore yet.
  • Scope sensitivity: By default, most people do not do a good job recognizing large differences in impact. In a classic study, “respondents were asked how much they were willing to pay to prevent migrating birds from drowning in uncovered oil ponds by covering the oil ponds with protective nets. Subjects were told that either 2,000, 20,000, or 200,000 migrating birds were affected annually, for which subjects reported they were willing to pay $80, $78, and $88, respectively.” We should recognize this bias within ourselves and do our best to avoid it. 
  • Understanding counterfactual impact: We want to make the world the best place it can be, meaning that we should think about what it would look like if we hadn’t taken a course of action. While a doctor may take many actions that save lives over the course of their career, it is often the case that most of these lives could have been saved by another doctor administering the same treatment. Additional doctors tend to spend time on less important, less certain procedures, and in the UK, another doctor may only counterfactually save about 3 lives total throughout their career. 

Given these considerations, effective altruists have long advocated for rigorous “cause prioritization,” thinking carefully about what matters most to help in the world. And, as powerful AI gets closer and closer, the philanthropic landscape is radically changing, and we must think carefully about how we can do the most good. 

This curriculum will give readers a starting point to address some of the most important considerations facing humanity this century, and what it means to “do the most good we can” in the age of AGI. 

Week 0: Will AI be transformative?

This week has some broader context on AI forecasting and capabilities. If you aren’t very familiar with this, you may want to spend some time looking over and thinking about these materials before you progress to later weeks, where we discuss the intersection of powerful AI and other causes in more depth. That being said, here are some of my recommended readings, as well as some highlights from them:

  • Will we have AGI by 2030? | 80,000 Hours (36 minute read; 3 minute intro)
    • “Four key factors are driving AI progress: larger base models, teaching models to reason, increasing models’ thinking time, and building agent scaffolding for multi-step tasks.     • “All of these drivers are set to continue until 2028 and perhaps until 2032.”
  • AI is probably not a bubble - by Peter Wildeford (13 minute read)
    • Peter Wildeford is a co-founder of the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, a co-founder of Rethink Priorities, the Head of Policy at the AI Policy Network, and a top superforecaster.
    • At EAG NYC 2026, Wildeford gave a talk following up on the predictions and thoughts he made in this post. That talk was called “AI is still not a bubble,” and it reviews Wildeford’s predictions and recent trends in AI development.
  • Data Bottlenecks Won’t Stop an Intelligence Explosion (23 minute read)
    • This essay does a good job describing the recursive self-improvement (RSI) process in depth, and it explores how various data bottlenecks might influence its trajectory.
  • The Power of Intelligence (5 minute read) 
    • Eliezer Yudkowsky’s classic 2007 essay about what intelligence can do to the world, and why we might expect it to be transformative.
  • How Accurate Have AI Progress Forecasts Been So Far? (20 minute read)
    • “Since mid-2022, FRI has collected forecasts on AI progress across many projects.     • Most of the previous readings in Week 0 are relatively bullish on AI progress. In the interest of representing a wide range of views, here’s a reading list compiling a more diverse range of perspectives on timelines and capabilities.

Week 1: The Search for the Most Important Problem

It’s hard to think of a question more important than, “What is the most important problem for us to work on?” It’s also hard to think of a more difficult question to answer. This week introduces background context for how to begin thinking about this question, mathematical reasons for why it’s difficult, and some strategies we can use to prepare ourselves for later weeks. 

Required Readings:

  • Small Groups of Correlated Researchers (7 minute read)
    • The intro essay to this series. We’re trying to discover the most important problem in the world, but the resources available to us are uniquely underpowered to give us a good answer. The burden of making a best guess therefore falls on us, but we shouldn’t feel too confident in even our best guesses. 
  • Strategies for learning - Andy Masley (19 minute read) 
    • A good post to prepare for a series where we intend to make progress on the most important question in the world. 
    • Emphasis on “commit to strong beliefs when you’re first learning about a new subject and then adjust them over time, instead of staying uncertain the whole time.”
  • Preparing for the Intelligence Explosion (31 minute read; 3 minute intro) (Sections 1, 2, 3, and the “Grand Challenges” part of Section 4, stopping before “AI takeover”)

Optional Readings:

  • Doing Prioritization Better — EA Forum (35 minute read; 1 minute executive summary)
    • Rather than just comparing causes, we might compare a variety of interventions across causes. Also, a bunch of helpful statistics about how many FTEs there are trying to solve various cause prioritization problems.
  • What We Owe The Future, Chapter 1 (25 minute read)
    • The basic case for longtermism and strong longtermism.
  • Strategic Cause Selection | Coefficient Giving (5 minute read)
    • A summary of the heuristics used by Coefficient Giving to decide which causes are worth supporting (they use importance, neglectedness, and tractability, along with a specific process for evaluating evidence behind the causes)
  • Cost-Effectiveness | Coefficient Giving (6 minute read) 
    • A summary of how Coefficient Giving determines which charities are highly cost-effective and allocates money to them (they create a metric called “Coefficient Giving dollars,” where one $CG is equivalent to “the benefit of giving $1 to someone earning $50,000 a year” and only funds charities that earn more than $CG 1000 per $1 donated)

    • Interrogating whether or not longtermist reasoning should be a crux for anyone who thinks existential risk is the most cost-effective cause to work on,
  • Exploring Key Cases with the Portfolio Builder - EA Forum (7 minute read)
    • Explores Rethink Priories’ cross-cause donation portfolio builder and shows how you should reallocate funds to maximize EV under different assumptions.
  • How bad would human extinction be? - EA Forum (26 minute read)
    • Attempts to estimate the true expected size of future human civilization based on a variety of assumptions about when we might go extinct.

    • A series that tries to find (and examine the implication of) a plausible moral view for cause prioritization, other than pure expected value maximization. 
  • The Moral Weight Project Sequence - EA Forum (401 minute read; 11 minute intro)  
    • A series that tries to figure out how we can compare the magnitude of valenced experience across different sentient creatures, and how uncertain we should be about this. 
  • The Unexpected Value of the Future | Ergo an Open Access Journal of Philosophy (50 minute read; 3 minute intro) 

Week 2: The Hinge of History?

Even if AI doesn’t lead to human extinction, small changes in the shape of progress and governance today could have enormous ramifications for millions of years to come. If this is the case, we might think the following decades will be a unique turning point in human history. Some have referred to this time as “the most important century” and “the hinge of history.”

This week will explore where we are now, how we can respond to changing circumstances, and what this could mean for the future. 

Required Readings:

  • Effective altruism in the age of AGI — EA Forum (24 minute read)
    • “EA should embrace the mission of making the transition to a post-AGI society go well, significantly expanding our cause area focus beyond traditional AI safety. This means working on neglected areas like AI welfare, AI character, AI persuasion and epistemic disruption, human power concentration, space governance, and more (while continuing work on global health, animal welfare, AI safety, and biorisk).”
  • AGI and Lock-in (30 minute read)
    • Sections:
      • All of section 0 except 0.2.2 (8 minutes)
      • All of section 1 (5 minutes)
      • All of section 2 (5 minutes)
      • All of section 3 (4 minutes)
      • All of section 8 (8 minutes)
    • “With sufficient investments, it will be feasible to develop AGI-based institutions that (with high probability) competently and faithfully pursue any such values until an external source stops them, or until the values in question imply that they should stop. If a large majority of the world’s economic and military powers agreed to set-up such an institution, and bestowed it with the power to defend itself against external threats, that institution could pursue its agenda for at least millions of years (and perhaps for trillions).”
  • The third wave of American philanthropy - by Nan Ransohoff (17 minute read)
    • “Hundreds of billions of dollars in new philanthropic capital will soon become liquid. The OpenAI Foundation holds 26% of OpenAI, worth about $220B at today’s valuation. Anthropic’s seven co-founders have pledged to give away 80% of their wealth and have instituted the most aggressive donor matching program for employees in tech history.”

Optional Readings:

  • The "most important century" introduction (9 minute read)
    • An overview of a series written by the founder of GiveWell, Holden Karnofsky, about the ways the future could be vastly different, based on the outcomes of the next several years. 
  • Are we living at the hinge of history? | Global Priorities Institute (50 minute read; 2 minute intro) 
    • Philosopher Will MacAskill’s 2020 analysis of the arguments for and against the idea that we’re living at a uniquely important moment in human history. 
  • Animal Welfare is Just Part of AI Alignment Now (30 minute read; 1 minute intro) 
    • Animal advocate Aidan Kankyoku’s reflections on the modern EA movement, its propensity to choose strange causes to pursue, its epistemic habits, and how a good vision for “Making AI Go Well” should include animal advocacy.
  • The Track Record of Futurists Seems ... Fine (14 minute read)
    • Keeping score of the predictions made by the futurists of the past. 

Week 3: Direct Risks from AI

Powerful AI, depending on the circumstances of how it’s created and whose ideals it follows, could radically alter the trajectory of civilization. But what, specifically, are these threats? And what can we do about them? 

This reading list assumes that you already have a good understanding of the classic “loss of control” AI risk scenario but less context on other threats or how to deal with them. If you are unfamiliar with loss of control risks already, we recommend that you read 80,000 Hours’ risk profile.

Required Readings:

  • Three Types of Intelligence Explosion (15 minute read) 
    • Read everything except the appendices
  • Plans A, B, C, and D for misalignment risk (8 minute read)
    • A discussion of how we may consider responding to existential and concentration of power risks from AI.
  • The Four Pillars: A Hypothesis for Countering Catastrophic Biological Risk (11 minute read)
    • How can we catch deadly pandemics early and respond to them? Is biosecurity solvable in the long run?
  • AI-Enabled Coups: How a Small Group Could Use AI to Seize Power (6 minute read)
    • Read the Abstract (1 minute) and Summary (5 minutes)
    • A list of three ways that powerful AI could empower small groups to gain disproportionate control of society, and why AI specifically could shift social dynamics to enable this to happen when it was previously difficult.
  • Gradual disempowerment | 80,000 Hours (7 minute read)
    • A brief intro to and discussion of a threat where human agency is disempowered by increasingly capable AI systems, which ultimately pursue goals that don’t support human interests as well as previous systems (such as markets or democracy).
  • The importance of AI character (12 minute read) 
    • Read Sections 0 (1 minute), 1 (6 minutes), and the appendices (4 minutes)
    • A discussion of the long-term implications of small differences in AI model character.

Optional Readings:

  • Loss of control | 80,000 Hours (46 minute read; 1 minute intro)
    • A good read for anyone not familiar with the case for why we think AIs might try to take over power from humans.
  • You Need A Theory of Victory - by Jason Hausenloy (13 minute read)
    • An outline of some of the different “AI safety worldviews,” their recommended courses of action, and the cruxes that differentiate them.

    • A proposal to decrease takeover from misaligned AI by making the models more risk-averse.

    • Discussions of how different AI governance strategies may affect various AI risk profiles.

    • A classic post describing a few scenarios of AI going poorly for humanity.

    • A response to Kulveit et al.’s paper discussing the idea of Gradual Disempowerment

    • An in-depth summary of the arguments surrounding AI consciousness, why it matters, and what we should consider doing about it.

    • A summary of the evidence that may lead you to believe that we need much more political will, rather than research.
  • How Can We Prevent AI-Enabled Coups? - by Forethought (134 minute listen) 
    • Podcast episode exploring how we can avoid extreme power concentration from AI-enabled coups

Required Readings:

  • The State of the AIxAnimals Field - by Itsi Weinstock (11 minute read)

    • This post contains a brief overview of the types of projects that become viable to improve animal welfare as AI becomes increasingly capable. 
  • Should Machine Gods Dream of Liberated Sheep? (30 minute read; 4 minute intro)
    • A key debate in AI alignment is whether AI should be a corrigible (always does what the user says) tool, or a morally reflective agent trying to make good decisions.   • Digital Consciousness Model Results and Key Takeaways  (7 minute read)
    • A model that attempts to estimate how we should update our probability that a creature is conscious, given behavioral evidence and priors about its consciousness. In this post, it is applied to both 2024 LLMs and historical AIs to test its calibration. 
  • AI and animal welfare: am I missing something? — EA Forum (3 minute read)
    • A post casting doubt on whether or not the “AIxAnimals” framing is helpful.
    • “Nobody is ‘ignoring’ animal welfare; they’re just indifferent. AI systems are being built to do exactly what they were designed to do, which is to faithfully execute human preferences. Optional Readings:

  • Preparing the Animal Movement for AGI - by Aidan Kankyoku (6 minute read)
    • A post raising awareness of the incoming potential of transformative AI and urging the animal welfare movement to prepare. 
  • Rethink Priorities’ Welfare Range Estimates (18 minute read) 
    • Classic post trying to estimate the difference in magnitudes of the maximum valenced experience across creatures. 
  • The impacts of AI on animal advocacy (12 minute read) 
    • A few specific details about how AI might affect farming conditions and uplift activists. Written in September 2025, so missing a lot of the recent increases in capabilities.
  • Can AI be Conscious? Biological Naturalism as a Research Program (54 minute read; 3 minute executive summary)
    • Rethink Priorities’ research report exploring whether or not “biological naturalism”, the viewpoint claiming that consciousness must arise from carbon-based structures, is correct.

In previous weeks, we discussed the idea of “AGI-induced lock-in,” the idea that a powerful-enough AI model could lead a single group to control the rest of the future of civilization. In this week, we will explore arguments about the tractability and effectiveness of supporting democratic systems in a time when transformative AI may be on the rise. 

MAIA chose this week’s readings because they offer useful information and perspectives worth discussing, not because our organizations agree with them. Some of them criticize specific politicians, parties, or policies. MAIA and EA@MIT are nonpartisan: we do not support or oppose any candidate or party, and we do not endorse any recommendations in the readings about how to vote, whom to donate to, or what legislation to support. Read everything here critically.

Required Readings:

  • Why Is Democracy Worth Defending? (8 minute read)
    • Outlines a seven-point case for why democracy may be worth defending: Democracy promotes greater well-being, better health, more human and civil rights, stronger social relationships, peace, egalitarianism, and quality governance. 
    • The evidence for some of these seven points is stronger than others.
  • American effective altruists should consider political donations (14 minute read)
    • A piece arguing that donations to political campaigns are of unusually high leverage in the next few years. It points out that donations directly to politicians receive certain cost-effectiveness bonuses that large donors cannot reach. 
  • Towards a longtermist framework for evaluating democracy-related interventions - Rethink Priorities (35 minute read; 4 minute intro)
    • This post describes the key features of liberal democracy (those being competitive democracy, accuracy, responsiveness, participation, voter competence, liberalism, and inclusion), discusses goals that longtermists may set as a response to these, and explores some of the implications for action that this may result in. 
  • The Surprising Tractability of US Politics (3 minute read)
    • Fundraising and talent recruitment programs can have drastic effects on elections because the default incentives in US politics motivate the most talented people to go elsewhere.

Optional Readings:

  • In search of a dynamist vision for safe superhuman AI (8 minute read)
    • Argues that a lot of ideal futures are “dynamist,” meaning flexible, fluid, and giving control to many, while a lot of current AI policy advocacy fights for “stasist” (meaning solidified) solutions.
    • “The classic AI risks—catastrophic misuse, catastrophic misalignment—could indeed be game over for dynamism, so we need to handle those. But if we handle them by massively concentrating power, we haven’t succeeded. For the future to actually go well, we will need to find our way to some new equilibrium that allows for decentralized experimentation, spontaneous adjustment, creativity, and risk-taking.” 
  • Extreme power concentration | 80,000 Hours (34 minute read; 1 minute intro)
    • The broad case for why we should worry about extreme power concentration, what we can do about it, and how neglected it is.

Week 6: Better Futures

Which is larger: the gap between extinction and a mediocre future, or the gap between a mediocre future and a flourishing future? Will any actions taken today reliably influence what happens much later? Can we prepare ourselves for a future beyond our solar system? Can we fight the spread of harmful misinformation?

Required Readings:

  • Introducing Better Futures (7 minute read) 
    • Why we should care about much more than just averting human extinction. In short, the gap between a flourishing future and a mediocre future might be much larger than the gap between a mediocre future and no future. 
  • Space governance | 80,000 Hours (31 minute read; 2 minute intro)
    • Early governance documents and agreements have the potential to have enormous influence on the far future of humanity. It could be exceptionally important to have more people researching this carefully.
  • Design Sketches: Collective Epistemics (18 minute read) 
    • Five proposals for projects that could improve worldwide epistemics. These are: community notes for everything, extreme rhetoric highlighting, speaker reliability tracking, “epistemic virtue” evals for frontier AI models, and provenance tracing (checking the reliability and robustness of claims).
  • Do not conquer what you cannot defend — LessWrong (7 minute read)
    • A broader lesson about the risks of starting institutions that are too powerful, an important consideration when discussing how to shape the future.  

Optional Readings:

  • How to Make the Future Better (38 minute read; 2 minute intro)
    • A concrete list of actions you can take, ending the Better Futures essay series.
  • Space Governance Plan (47 minute read; 2 minute summary) 
    • An appendix to AI 2040: Plan A that reviews several different proposals for how space governance may work.
  • AI for epistemics (12 minute read)
    • A supplement to AI 2040: Plan A that adds to the list of ideas outlined in the Forethought Design Sketches, introduces the idea of “epistemic basins” (futures where community epistemics get locked into being good or bad), lists the places where good epistemics are most important, and gives some example interventions to support these. 
  • Forecasting is Way Overrated, and We Should Stop Funding It — EA Forum (6 minute read)
    • An argument that forecasting doesn’t produce helpful results or inform decision making enough to justify the amount of funding it receives.
  • Response to Forecasting is Way Overrated (11 minute read)
    • A response to the previous post, giving additional insight into the things that forecasting has been valuable for. 

Other extended reading lists:

Everything:

  • Astra futurism reading list 
  • My Recommendations for a Diverse Range of AI Timelines Perspectives 

AIxAnimals:

  • SF AI×Animals 
  • Digital Minds: A Quickstart Guide 

Cause Prioritization:

  • The Moral Weight Project Sequence - EA Forum 
  • The CURVE Sequence - EA Forum

While creating this reading list, I tried my best to ensure that all the required readings were enjoyable, information-dense, and discussable. For the most part, I also tried to remove duplicate content. This is less true for the optional readings, but there's still a lot of great stuff there. It turns out that the EA community is pretty fantastic and flush with ideas! Still, if anyone has thoughts about serious oversights in this list or ways to improve it while keeping the required readings below 1 hour per week, I'd love to hear it. 

There is also a version of this doc with prettier formatting.

What is this?

Effective Altruism has long sought to answer the question, “How do I do the most good with the resources available to me?” From this question, it has trended toward several patterns of thinking, as it has found those styles to be most helpful for answering these questions:

  • Comparing differences in impact: The most cost-effective interventions are often vastly more impactful than the median ones, and time spent prioritizing between areas can lead to actions that do vastly more good than others
  • Recognizing triage: Any hour that we spend working on one project is necessarily not spent dedicated to another project, and any amount of money donated to one charity is necessarily not given to another. We’re constantly choosing not to support a variety of important interventions and causes, and we should consider that sacrifice as we decide what is worth working on. 
  • Recognizing the differences between “fuzzies” and “utilons”: Interventions that may intuitively appeal to us might (“fuzzies”) not be the ones that help the most (“utilons”), or that really treat others with the dignity of equality.
  • The Scout Mindset: Rather than seek to defend positions that we already hold, like a soldier defending their territory, we should try to create an accurate map of reality that helps us make better decisions. 
  • Thinking at the margin: When we ask ourselves the question, “What ought we to do?”, we are not asking the question, “What should everyone in the world do?”. Our decisions should be informed by our particular circumstances and the full effects of our decisions alone. For example, at the current margin, an additional cancer researcher does not make very much progress toward curing cancer, while a single person working on early detection for deadly pandemics could be responsible for breakthroughs that the field’s limited resources haven’t had time to explore yet.

    • Rather than just comparing causes, we might compare a variety of interventions across causes. Also, a bunch of helpful statistics about how many FTEs there are trying to solve various cause prioritization problems.
  • What We Owe The Future, Chapter 1 (25 minute read)
    • The basic case for longtermism and strong longtermism.
  • Strategic Cause Selection | Coefficient Giving (5 minute read)
    • A summary of the heuristics used by Coefficient Giving to decide which causes are worth supporting (they use importance, neglectedness, and tractability, along with a specific process for evaluating evidence behind the causes)
  • Cost-Effectiveness | Coefficient Giving (6 minute read) 
    • A summary of how Coefficient Giving determines which charities are highly cost-effective and allocates money to them (they create a metric called “Coefficient Giving dollars,” where one $CG is equivalent to “the benefit of giving $1 to someone earning $50,000 a year” and only funds charities that earn more than $CG 1000 per $1 donated)
  • Is x-risk the most cost-effective if we count only the next few generations? - EA Forum (21 minute read)
    • Interrogating whether or not longtermist reasoning should be a crux for anyone who thinks existential risk is the most cost-effective cause to work on,
  • Exploring Key Cases with the Portfolio Builder - EA Forum (7 minute read)
    • Explores Rethink Priories’ cross-cause donation portfolio builder and shows how you should reallocate funds to maximize EV under different assumptions.
  • How bad would human extinction be? - EA Forum (26 minute read)
    • Attempts to estimate the true expected size of future human civilization based on a variety of assumptions about when we might go extinct. 
  • The CURVE Sequence - EA Forum (234 minute read; 18 minute intro)
    • A series that tries to find (and examine the implication of) a plausible moral view for cause prioritization, other than pure expected value maximization. 
  • The Moral Weight Project Sequence - EA Forum (401 minute read; 11 minute intro)  
    • A series that tries to figure out how we can compare the magnitude of valenced experience across different sentient creatures, and how uncertain we should be about this. 
  • The Unexpected Value of the Future | Ergo an Open Access Journal of Philosophy (50 minute read; 3 minute intro) 

Week 2: The Hinge of History?

We may be living in a moment uniquely powerful for shaping the rest of human history. Even if AI doesn’t lead to human extinction, small changes in the shape of progress and governance today could have enormous ramifications for millions of years to come. If this is the case, we might think the following decades will be a unique turning point in human history. Some have referred to this time as “the most important century” and “the hinge of history.”

This week will explore where we are now, how we can respond to changing circumstances, and what this could mean for the future. 

Required Readings:

  • Effective altruism in the age of AGI — EA Forum (24 minute read)
    • “EA should embrace the mission of making the transition to a post-AGI society go well, significantly expanding our cause area focus beyond traditional AI safety. This means working on neglected areas like AI welfare, AI character, AI persuasion and epistemic disruption, human power concentration, space governance, and more (while continuing work on global health, animal welfare, AI safety, and biorisk).”
  • AGI and Lock-in (30 minute read)
    • Sections:
      • All of section 0 except 0.2.2 (8 minutes)
      • All of section 1 (5 minutes)
      • All of section 2 (5 minutes)
      • All of section 3 (4 minutes)
      • All of section 8 (8 minutes)
    • “With sufficient investments, it will be feasible to develop AGI-based institutions that (with high probability) competently and faithfully pursue any such values until an external source stops them, or until the values in question imply that they should stop. If a large majority of the world’s economic and military powers agreed to set-up such an institution, and bestowed it with the power to defend itself against external threats, that institution could pursue its agenda for at least millions of years (and perhaps for trillions).”
  • The third wave of American philanthropy - by Nan Ransohoff (17 minute read)
    • “Hundreds of billions of dollars in new philanthropic capital will soon become liquid. The OpenAI Foundation holds 26% of OpenAI, worth about $220B at today’s valuation. Anthropic’s seven co-founders have pledged to give away 80% of their wealth and have instituted the most aggressive donor matching program for employees in tech history.”

Optional Readings:

  • The "most important century" introduction (9 minute read)
    • An overview of a series written by the founder of GiveWell, Holden Karnofsky, about the ways the future could be vastly different, based on the outcomes of the next several years. 
  • Are we living at the hinge of history? | Global Priorities Institute (50 minute read; 2 minute intro) 
    • Philosopher Will MacAskill’s 2020 analysis of the arguments for and against the idea that we’re living at a uniquely important moment in human history. 
  • Animal Welfare is Just Part of AI Alignment Now (30 minute read; 1 minute intro) 
    • Animal advocate Aidan Kankyoku’s reflections on the modern EA movement, its propensity to choose strange causes to pursue, its epistemic habits, and how a good vision for “Making AI Go Well” should include animal advocacy.
  • The Track Record of Futurists Seems ... Fine (14 minute read)
    • Keeping score of the predictions made by the futurists of the past. 

Week 3: Direct Risks from AI

Powerful AI, depending on the circumstances of how it’s created and whose ideals it follows, could radically alter the trajectory of civilization. But what, specifically, are these threats? And what can we do about them? 

This reading list assumes that you already have a good understanding of the classic “loss of control” AI risk scenario but less context on other threats or how to deal with them. If you are unfamiliar with loss of control risks already, we recommend that you read 80,000 Hours’ risk profile.

Required Readings:

  • Three Types of Intelligence Explosion (15 minute read) 
    • Read everything except the appendices
  • Plans A, B, C, and D for misalignment risk (8 minute read)
    • A discussion of how we may consider responding to existential and concentration of power risks from AI.
  • The Four Pillars: A Hypothesis for Countering Catastrophic Biological Risk (11 minute read)
    • How can we catch deadly pandemics early and respond to them? Is biosecurity solvable in the long run?
  • AI-Enabled Coups: How a Small Group Could Use AI to Seize Power (6 minute read)
    • Read the Abstract (1 minute) and Summary (5 minutes)
    • A list of three ways that powerful AI could empower small groups to gain disproportionate control of society, and why AI specifically could shift social dynamics to enable this to happen when it was previously difficult.
  • Gradual disempowerment | 80,000 Hours (7 minute read)
    • A brief intro to and discussion of a threat where human agency is disempowered by increasingly capable AI systems, which ultimately pursue goals that don’t support human interests as well as previous systems (such as markets or democracy).
  • The importance of AI character (12 minute read) 
    • Read Sections 0 (1 minute), 1 (6 minutes), and the appendices (4 minutes)
    • A discussion of the long-term implications of small differences in AI model character.

Optional Readings:

  • Loss of control | 80,000 Hours (46 minute read; 1 minute intro)
    • A good read for anyone not familiar with the case for why we think AIs might try to take over power from humans.
  • You Need A Theory of Victory - by Jason Hausenloy (13 minute read)
    • An outline of some of the different “AI safety worldviews,” their recommended courses of action, and the cruxes that differentiate them.  
  • AI 2027 (107 minute read; 55 minutes before the two endings)
    • A classic 2025 report forecasting the next several years of AI progress and briefly outlining how this could go very well or very poorly for humanity. The authors include:
      • Daniel Kokotajlo, a former AI researcher known for forecasting “What 2026 looks like” and for taking a large risk to his vested equities by refusing to sign OpenAI’s non-disparagement agreement upon leaving, so he could speak out about their risky behavior.
      • Eli Lifland, one of the top all-time superforecasters on the RAND Forecasting Initiative leaderboard.
      • Several other researchers and forecasters, who, along with Kokotajlo and Lifland, comprise the AI Futures Project.
  • Risk-Averse AIs (51 minute read; 5 minute intro)
    • A proposal to decrease takeover from misaligned AI by making the models more risk-averse.
  • Strategic visions in AI governance: Mapping pathways to victory — Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (46 minute read; 2 minute executive summary)
    • Discussions of how different AI governance strategies may affect various AI risk profiles. 
  • What failure looks like — LessWrong (10 minute read)
    • A classic post describing a few scenarios of AI going poorly for humanity. 
  • S-risks: An introduction (10 minute read)
    • An introduction to the philosophical idea of “suffering risks,” the potential for futures containing extreme amounts of suffering, and why we should try to avoid them.
  • A Critique of Gradual Disempowerment (9 minute read)
    • A response to Kulveit et al.’s paper discussing the idea of Gradual Disempowerment 
  • Moral status of digital minds | 80,000 Hours (47 minute read; 1 minute intro) 
    • An in-depth summary of the arguments surrounding AI consciousness, why it matters, and what we should consider doing about it. 
  • The current bottleneck is political will, not research (28 minute read)
    • A summary of the evidence that may lead you to believe that we need much more political will, rather than research.
  • How Can We Prevent AI-Enabled Coups? - by Forethought (134 minute listen) 
    • Podcast episode exploring how we can avoid extreme power concentration from AI-enabled coups

Week 4: AGI and Animals

The best future is one where all sentient creatures get to live a good life. But are there any tractable interventions that could bring us closer to that future? And how could transformative AI shift these dynamics?

Required Readings:

  • The State of the AIxAnimals Field - by Itsi Weinstock (11 minute read)
    • A post explaining the size of the field (small), who’s involved (about two full orgs and some partial help from other groups), and what they want to accomplish (measure how AI is integrated into factory farming, motivate AIs to directly consider and talk about animal welfare, and modify legislation to also include clauses about welfare-favoring AI behavior) as of April 2026. There’s also a list of suggested projects.
  • Request for Proposals for AI x Animals — EA Forum (5 minute read) 
    • This post contains a brief overview of the types of projects that become viable to improve animal welfare as AI becomes increasingly capable. 
  • Should Machine Gods Dream of Liberated Sheep? (30 minute read; 4 minute intro)
    • A key debate in AI alignment is whether AI should be a corrigible (always does what the user says) tool, or a morally reflective agent trying to make good decisions. In this post, Aidan Kankyoku, a major figure in the animal rights movement, discusses the implications of this discussion for the future of animal wellbeing. 
  • Digital Consciousness Model Results and Key Takeaways  (7 minute read)
    • A model that attempts to estimate how we should update our probability that a creature is conscious, given behavioral evidence and priors about its consciousness. In this post, it is applied to both 2024 LLMs and historical AIs to test its calibration. 
  • AI and animal welfare: am I missing something? — EA Forum (3 minute read)
    • A post casting doubt on whether or not the “AIxAnimals” framing is helpful.
    • “Nobody is ‘ignoring’ animal welfare; they’re just indifferent. AI systems are being built to do exactly what they were designed to do, which is to faithfully execute human preferences. And those are, in aggregate, to eat cheap meat, conduct research on living organisms when it’s convenient, and prioritise cost and efficiency in agricultural supply chains. AI is reflecting the values of humans. I don’t think you can sneak those values in, unless there are specific opportunities to tweak things here and there before they get cemented.”

Optional Readings:

  • Preparing the Animal Movement for AGI - by Aidan Kankyoku (6 minute read)
    • A post raising awareness of the incoming potential of transformative AI and urging the animal welfare movement to prepare. 
  • Rethink Priorities’ Welfare Range Estimates (18 minute read) 
    • Classic post trying to estimate the difference in magnitudes of the maximum valenced experience across creatures. 
  • The impacts of AI on animal advocacy (12 minute read) 
    • A few specific details about how AI might affect farming conditions and uplift activists. Written in September 2025, so missing a lot of the recent increases in capabilities.
  • Can AI be Conscious? Biological Naturalism as a Research Program (54 minute read; 3 minute executive summary)
    • Rethink Priorities’ research report exploring whether or not “biological naturalism”, the viewpoint claiming that consciousness must arise from carbon-based structures, is correct.

Week 5: Democracy Preservation in the Face of Transformative Technology

In previous weeks, we discussed the idea of “AGI-induced lock-in,” the idea that a powerful-enough AI model could lead a single group to control the rest of the future of civilization. In this week, we will explore arguments about the tractability and effectiveness of supporting democratic systems in a time when transformative AI may be on the rise. 

MAIA chose this week’s readings because they offer useful information and perspectives worth discussing, not because our organizations agree with them. Some of them criticize specific politicians, parties, or policies. MAIA and EA@MIT are nonpartisan: we do not support or oppose any candidate or party, and we do not endorse any recommendations in the readings about how to vote, whom to donate to, or what legislation to support. Read everything here critically.

Required Readings:

  • Why Is Democracy Worth Defending? (8 minute read)
    • Outlines a seven-point case for why democracy may be worth defending: Democracy promotes greater well-being, better health, more human and civil rights, stronger social relationships, peace, egalitarianism, and quality governance. 
    • The evidence for some of these seven points is stronger than others.
  • American effective altruists should consider political donations (14 minute read)
    • A piece arguing that donations to political campaigns are of unusually high leverage in the next few years. It points out that donations directly to politicians receive certain cost-effectiveness bonuses that large donors cannot reach. 
  • Towards a longtermist framework for evaluating democracy-related interventions - Rethink Priorities (35 minute read; 4 minute intro)
    • This post describes the key features of liberal democracy (those being competitive democracy, accuracy, responsiveness, participation, voter competence, liberalism, and inclusion), discusses goals that longtermists may set as a response to these, and explores some of the implications for action that this may result in. 
  • The Surprising Tractability of US Politics (3 minute read)
    • Fundraising and talent recruitment programs can have drastic effects on elections because the default incentives in US politics motivate the most talented people to go elsewhere.

Optional Readings:

  • In search of a dynamist vision for safe superhuman AI (8 minute read)
    • Argues that a lot of ideal futures are “dynamist,” meaning flexible, fluid, and giving control to many, while a lot of current AI policy advocacy fights for “stasist” (meaning solidified) solutions.
    • “The classic AI risks—catastrophic misuse, catastrophic misalignment—could indeed be game over for dynamism, so we need to handle those. But if we handle them by massively concentrating power, we haven’t succeeded. For the future to actually go well, we will need to find our way to some new equilibrium that allows for decentralized experimentation, spontaneous adjustment, creativity, and risk-taking.” 
  • Extreme power concentration | 80,000 Hours (34 minute read; 1 minute intro)
    • The broad case for why we should worry about extreme power concentration, what we can do about it, and how neglected it is.

Week 6: Better Futures

Which is larger: the gap between extinction and a mediocre future, or the gap between a mediocre future and a flourishing future? Will any actions taken today reliably influence what happens much later? Can we prepare ourselves for a future beyond our solar system? Can we fight the spread of harmful misinformation?

Required Readings:

  • Introducing Better Futures (7 minute read) 
    • Why we should care about much more than just averting human extinction. In short, the gap between a flourishing future and a mediocre future might be much larger than the gap between a mediocre future and no future. 
  • Space governance | 80,000 Hours (31 minute read; 2 minute intro)
    • Early governance documents and agreements have the potential to have enormous influence on the far future of humanity. It could be exceptionally important to have more people researching this carefully.
  • Design Sketches: Collective Epistemics (18 minute read) 
    • Five proposals for projects that could improve worldwide epistemics. These are: community notes for everything, extreme rhetoric highlighting, speaker reliability tracking, “epistemic virtue” evals for frontier AI models, and provenance tracing (checking the reliability and robustness of claims).
  • Do not conquer what you cannot defend — LessWrong (7 minute read)
    • A broader lesson about the risks of starting institutions that are too powerful, an important consideration when discussing how to shape the future.  

Optional Readings:

  • How to Make the Future Better (38 minute read; 2 minute intro)
    • A concrete list of actions you can take, ending the Better Futures essay series.
  • Space Governance Plan (47 minute read; 2 minute summary) 
    • An appendix to AI 2040: Plan A that reviews several different proposals for how space governance may work.
  • AI for epistemics (12 minute read)
    • A supplement to AI 2040: Plan A that adds to the list of ideas outlined in the Forethought Design Sketches, introduces the idea of “epistemic basins” (futures where community epistemics get locked into being good or bad), lists the places where good epistemics are most important, and gives some example interventions to support these. 
  • Forecasting is Way Overrated, and We Should Stop Funding It — EA Forum (6 minute read)
    • An argument that forecasting doesn’t produce helpful results or inform decision making enough to justify the amount of funding it receives.
  • Response to Forecasting is Way Overrated (11 minute read)
    • A response to the previous post, giving additional insight into the things that forecasting has been valuable for. 

Other extended reading lists:

Everything:

  • Astra futurism reading list 
  • My Recommendations for a Diverse Range of AI Timelines Perspectives 

AIxAnimals:

  • SF AI×Animals 
  • Digital Minds: A Quickstart Guide 

Cause Prioritization:

  • The Moral Weight Project Sequence - EA Forum 
  • The CURVE Sequence - EA Forum
