item.title: If no one builds it, trillions die
item.description:
Published on October 27, 2026 11:57 AM GMT

Unless plant-based or cultivated meat reaches taste and price parity with conventional meat, the amount of farm animal suffering will grow, with no end in sight.

If we succeed with plant-based meat, we can significantly decrease conventional meat production and the suffering it causes. If we succeed with cultivated meat, we have a real shot at eliminating industrial animal agriculture.[1]

Even if we fall short of that goal, every 10 percent of conventional meat that we displace spares about 22 billion vertebrate animals a year, cuts about 1 billion metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions, spares roughly 130 million hectares of land from grazing animals or growing animal feed, pulls about 10,000 metric tons of medically relevant antibiotics out of the food chain, slashes naturally occurring pandemic risk, and more.

For anyone who wants to make the world better, this is a chance to help solve some of its biggest problems. The obstacles are real. So is the cost of waiting.

Since I'm writing for the EA Forum, I'll focus on animals.

The number of animals farmed and slaughtered for human food is staggering, and it keeps growing.

Every year, humanity farms and slaughters roughly 220 billion vertebrate animals for food: about 88 billion land animals (90 percent of them chickens) and another 130 billion farmed fish.[2] That’s more animals every year than the total number of humans who have ever lived.

And those numbers keep climbing, setting new global records almost every year since 1961, when the UN FAO started keeping track (there's been exactly one down year for farmed fish, and not a single down year for land animals).[3] 

In the four decades since I adopted a vegan diet, global land animal meat production has more than doubled, and the number of slaughtered land animals has more than tripled (because of the small-body problem: disproportionate increases in chicken consumption, and chickens are small). The number of farmed fish has grown roughly tenfold over a slightly shorter timeframe.

It’s impossible for the human mind to grasp numbers this big or suffering at this scale. But it’s worth trying, because every single one of these 220 billion animals matters as much as any cat or dog we know personally, and almost all of them are leading lives of misery and then dying horribly. 

Alternative proteins are our best (and perhaps only) hope to reduce the number of animals farmed and slaughtered for food. 

Plant-based and cultivated meat are to animal agriculture what renewable energy and electric vehicles are to fossil fuels and gas-powered cars: market-based solutions that change how we meet demand. The world is going to consume more energy and drive more miles as it gets wealthier. It’s also going to eat more meat. That’s why we need renewable energy, EVs, and alternative meats. 

The goal of these supply-side interventions is to give people what they want, made differently and at a lower price: In addition to encouraging consumers to us less energy, drive less, and eat less or no meat, we can change how energy is produced, cars are powered, and meat is made. The trick is to eliminate what Bill Gates calls "the green premium": the difference in price and experience between the more environmentally friendly product and its conventional counterpart.[4]

Why diet change advocacy is not enough

For more than half a century, environmentalists, doctors, nutritionists, and animal activists have begged the public to eat less meat. Those efforts have surely slowed the growth of meat consumption, and I would like to see them continue and improve.[5]

But they have not reversed the long-term rise in global meat production (they have not come anywhere close), and it’s hard to imagine that changing. Even in the United States, the top 10 years for meat production are the most recent 10. And all projections of global meat consumption into the future agree that, barring a global recession or something similar, both per capita and total meat consumption will keep rising through at least 2050.[6]

So let's take a page from the environmental movement: Let's figure out how to make meat that consumers love, but less expensive and without the suffering.[7]

The goal: Plant-based and cultivated meats that taste the same or better and cost the same or less, compared to conventional meats

Study after study finds that deliciousness and affordability are the top factors that drive food choices generally, as well as enthusiasm (or, more accurately right now, lack of enthusiasm) for plant-based and cultivated meat in particular.

The supply-side approach scales in a way nothing else does: Diet-focused progress has to be won over and over and over--person by person, cafeteria by cafeteria, or government by government. A campaign that works in Germany or Denmark has to be rebuilt everywhere else. There's not a market mechanism that will cause success in one area to naturally scale to other areas. 

With alternative proteins, the hard problems are taste and price, and those are science and engineering problems. Solve them once, and industry and governments everywhere have reasons to spread them globally: profits and more robust and resilient supply chains for companies, GDP and food security for countries, as I discuss in chapters 9 and 10 of my recently released book Meat, which Publishers Weekly named a top ten new release in science earlier this year.

We’ve seen this before: The price of solar panels has fallen by 99.7 percent over the past fifty years and by 63.5 percent in the last ten, because the US, Japan, Germany, and China invested in it. Today countries that spent nothing at all on the research are building solar farms at prices very few people predicted just 10 years ago.[8] The Human Genome Project was funded mainly by the US government and carried out by 20 institutions in 6 countries. Its results were made public and now underpin medicine everywhere.[9] We can do the same thing for meat, with public investment in open-access research (GFI’s top priority worldwide). 

Eliminating the most egregious abuses is important, but it’s not enough.

One area where advocates are making progress is farm animal welfare. And make no mistake: If you were a hen in a cage or a mother pig in a crate, you would want advocates working hard to get you out. I am extremely supportive of this work, which earns a significant chunk of my personal philanthropy. 

But getting rid of the worst abuses (through welfare campaigns) and reducing the number of animals subjected to any abuse at all (through alternative proteins) accomplish different things. 

Welfare improvements are deeply meaningful, but even with them, conditions on industrial farms stay atrocious, both physically and mentally. These improvements matter so much precisely because conditions are the stuff of nightmares, whether for animals on land or in water. 

Welfare wins are also hard to scale globally. Most have come in the United States and the European Union, which account for about one-fifth of land animals slaughtered (17.3 of 87.9 billion) and just north of 1 percent of aquaculture (1.5 of 141 million metric tons).[10] Winning elsewhere is harder, and a victory in one country does not carry over to the next. 

So we need both: reducing the suffering of animals on farms now through welfare campaigns, and reducing the number of animals farmed through alternative meats that reach taste and price parity with conventional meat. Plant-based meat can substantially decrease the number of animals factory farmed, and cultivated meat has a real shot at cutting that number to zero, as I discuss here.

The Forum’s top two questions: Will it work, and will people eat it? 

Two questions about alternative meats recur most often on the EA Forum: Can plant-based and cultivated meat reach taste and price parity with conventional meat? And if they do, will people eat them? My first two Meat Matters articles tackle these questions. Here are the short versions: 

Scientific viability: More than 100 companies and hundreds of university scientists around the world are working to get cultivated meat to taste and price parity; those numbers are up from one (Upside Foods) and two (Mark Post and Marianne Ellis) just 11 years ago. At that point, Upside had raised just $125,000, which was all the private funding cultivated meat had ever received. Since then, costs have fallen by orders of magnitude, government funding and scientific progress have surged, and cultivated meat has gone from a $330,000 burger to full meals served to hundreds of people. I talk about why that's all quite mind-blowing in my first Meat Matters post. 

This feels a lot like solar and EVs a decade ago, when solar reached one percent of global electricity generation and EVs reached one percent of new car sales. For some cultivated meat companies, the central challenges now are regulatory approvals and securing the financing required to scale production. Those challenges are substantial, and success is far from certain, but the progress is deeply encouraging.[11]

Consumer acceptance: Consumer research suggests substantial interest in plant-based and cultivated meat, with good reason to expect that interest to grow further once products compete on taste and price (no product comes close right now).[12] At that point, benefits for food safety, the environment, global health, and animals can become additional reasons to choose them. On top of that, the economic and food security benefits give the meat industry and governments strong incentives to send price- and taste-competitive alt meats shooting up the adoption S-curve. I develop this argument here.

Will AGI or TAI solve cultivated meat? Let's make it happen! 

Some effective altruists expect artificial general intelligence (AGI) or transformative AI (TAI) to solve the taste and price challenges for alternative meats, and so they wonder: What's the point of work on alternative meats now? 

I’d love for that to happen, but I see at least three problems with waiting for it.

First, I’m not at all sure it’s true, absent significant effort from those of us who want to ensure that it happens. And as Lewis Bollard explained to Dwarkesh Patel, AI will also accelerate industrial animal farming. Unsurprisingly, AI is already making factory farming more efficient, and cheaper conventional meat makes competing on price harder.

Second, work we do now can make alternative proteins easier to advance with AI. We need much better data before machine learning can be maximally useful, we need trained scientists, and we need functioning companies. And then technical breakthroughs still have to become products: Facilities need financing, production needs scaling, and products need regulatory approval. They also need political support and the public’s trust. All of that requires an ecosystem, and that requires work right now. 

Third, speed matters. Every month, more than 18 billion vertebrate animals are farmed and slaughtered, each capable of feeling pain in much the same way we do. Animal scientist (and slaughterhouse designer) Temple Grandin has argued that they feel fear much more intensely than we do; in many cases, it’s incapacitatingly bad. And bioethicist Bernard Rollin has argued that pain may be worse for non-human animals, because they don’t know that it will end; in the moment, their suffering is their entire world.

My AI dream: a frontier lab takes on cultivated meat

Rather than wait for AGI to make meat without animals, let’s ask the people building it to help now. The science and engineering have advanced far enough that I think a frontier lab (e.g., the life sciences teams at Anthropic or OpenAI, or Google DeepMind) could solve the core challenges of making cultivated meat affordable, as I discuss here (and in much more depth in Meat). 

With their budgets, expertise, and connections, they could build the science and engineering roadmap for cheap cultivated meat and hand it to the world. With a bit more investment, they could speed up today’s startups or launch new ones, creating a thriving cultivated meat industry.

Most of the labs’ life sciences work focuses on medicine, and that work matters. But cultivated meat is a biology problem too, and solving it would end more suffering than almost anything else they could take on: hundreds of billions of vertebrate animals a year. 

And think about how cool it would be to change the very nature of nature by removing the need for live animals as a precursor to the production of animal meat.[13]

If you’re at a frontier lab and want to talk about making this happen, please get in touch. 

There is no plan B for reducing farm animal numbers, so let’s go all-in on alternative proteins.

If alternative meats fail, trillions more vertebrate animals will live miserable lives and die painful, terrifying deaths. Even if success were inevitable eventually (and I don't think it is), speed is a moral imperative: Every second, the world slaughters 2,800 land animals and 4,100 farmed finfish.

I believe that cultivated meat could eventually replace all industrial animal meat. But we don’t have to get anywhere near that goal to make an enormous difference. Displacing even 1 percent of conventional meat production means 2.2 billion fewer vertebrate animals each year living and dying in misery. 

I think a lot about the history of science and engineering, and how much progress has depended on hundreds of people each making specific choices at specific moments. In retrospect, breakthroughs can look inevitable. But behind them are people who chose to work on a difficult problem, fund an uncertain idea, or champion a technology before its promise was obvious.

In 2015, the International Energy Agency expected electric vehicles to remain a small share of the global car fleet through at least 2040. Why? In the IEA’s words, “the cost of batteries, consumer caution and limited recharging infrastructure.” Yet in 2025, electric cars made up 25 percent of new car sales worldwide and almost 55 percent in China, up from less than 1 percent a decade earlier.

How did that happen? Government policies in Europe, China, and the United States drove down battery costs, improved range, and paid for charging networks. Since 2015, battery prices have fallen about 75 percent, typical range has more than tripled, and the world has built more than 7 million public chargers. And companies, starting with Tesla, built cars good enough to shatter stereotypes about EVs and the people who drive them. 



Follow the chain back and you’ll find that dozens of people were instrumental, starting with Elon Musk, but also: the engineers at a tiny California company who showed Musk an electric sports car built on laptop batteries, the California regulators whose mandate gave Tesla billions in credits, everyone behind the controversial federal loan program that lent Tesla $465 million and saved the company from bankruptcy, the Chinese officials who helped Musk build a massive Tesla factory in 11 months (at a fraction of what it would have cost almost anywhere else), the three Nobel-winning chemists who made lithium-ion batteries possible, and so many more. 

The same is true for solar energy, mRNA vaccines, penicillin, and the Human Genome Project, stories I tell in chapter 8 of Meat, which Rachel Bronson, former president and CEO of the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, wrote in the Bulletin "should be required reading for anyone interested in scientific progress."

By Bruce Friedrich 🔸

Published on October 27, 2026 11:57 AM GMT

Unless plant-based or cultivated meat reaches taste and price parity with conventional meat, the amount of farm animal suffering will grow, with no end in sight.

If we succeed with plant-based meat, we can significantly decrease conventional meat production and the suffering it causes. If we succeed with cultivated meat, we have a real shot at eliminating industrial animal agriculture.[1]

Even if we fall short of that goal, every 10 percent of conventional meat that we displace spares about 22 billion vertebrate animals a year, cuts about 1 billion metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions, spares roughly 130 million hectares of land from grazing animals or growing animal feed, pulls about 10,000 metric tons of medically relevant antibiotics out of the food chain, slashes naturally occurring pandemic risk, and more.

For anyone who wants to make the world better, this is a chance to help solve some of its biggest problems. The obstacles are real. So is the cost of waiting.

Since I'm writing for the EA Forum, I'll focus on animals.

The number of animals farmed and slaughtered for human food is staggering, and it keeps growing.

Every year, humanity farms and slaughters roughly 220 billion vertebrate animals for food: about 88 billion land animals (90 percent of them chickens) and another 130 billion farmed fish.[2] That’s more animals every year than the total number of humans who have ever lived.

And those numbers keep climbing, setting new global records almost every year since 1961, when the UN FAO started keeping track (there's been exactly one down year for farmed fish, and not a single down year for land animals).[3] 

In the four decades since I adopted a vegan diet, global land animal meat production has more than doubled, and the number of slaughtered land animals has more than tripled (because of the small-body problem: disproportionate increases in chicken consumption, and chickens are small). The number of farmed fish has grown roughly tenfold over a slightly shorter timeframe.

It’s impossible for the human mind to grasp numbers this big or suffering at this scale. But it’s worth trying, because every single one of these 220 billion animals matters as much as any cat or dog we know personally, and almost all of them are leading lives of misery and then dying horribly. 

Alternative proteins are our best (and perhaps only) hope to reduce the number of animals farmed and slaughtered for food. 

Plant-based and cultivated meat are to animal agriculture what renewable energy and electric vehicles are to fossil fuels and gas-powered cars: market-based solutions that change how we meet demand. The world is going to consume more energy and drive more miles as it gets wealthier. It’s also going to eat more meat. That’s why we need renewable energy, EVs, and alternative meats. 

The goal of these supply-side interventions is to give people what they want, made differently and at a lower price: In addition to encouraging consumers to us less energy, drive less, and eat less or no meat, we can change how energy is produced, cars are powered, and meat is made. The trick is to eliminate what Bill Gates calls "the green premium": the difference in price and experience between the more environmentally friendly product and its conventional counterpart.[4]

Why diet change advocacy is not enough

For more than half a century, environmentalists, doctors, nutritionists, and animal activists have begged the public to eat less meat. Those efforts have surely slowed the growth of meat consumption, and I would like to see them continue and improve.[5]

But they have not reversed the long-term rise in global meat production (they have not come anywhere close), and it’s hard to imagine that changing. Even in the United States, the top 10 years for meat production are the most recent 10. And all projections of global meat consumption into the future agree that, barring a global recession or something similar, both per capita and total meat consumption will keep rising through at least 2050.[6]

So let's take a page from the environmental movement: Let's figure out how to make meat that consumers love, but less expensive and without the suffering.[7]

The goal: Plant-based and cultivated meats that taste the same or better and cost the same or less, compared to conventional meats

Study after study finds that deliciousness and affordability are the top factors that drive food choices generally, as well as enthusiasm (or, more accurately right now, lack of enthusiasm) for plant-based and cultivated meat in particular.

The supply-side approach scales in a way nothing else does: Diet-focused progress has to be won over and over and over--person by person, cafeteria by cafeteria, or government by government. A campaign that works in Germany or Denmark has to be rebuilt everywhere else. There's not a market mechanism that will cause success in one area to naturally scale to other areas. 

With alternative proteins, the hard problems are taste and price, and those are science and engineering problems. Solve them once, and industry and governments everywhere have reasons to spread them globally: profits and more robust and resilient supply chains for companies, GDP and food security for countries, as I discuss in chapters 9 and 10 of my recently released book Meat, which Publishers Weekly named a top ten new release in science earlier this year.

We’ve seen this before: The price of solar panels has fallen by 99.7 percent over the past fifty years and by 63.5 percent in the last ten, because the US, Japan, Germany, and China invested in it. Today countries that spent nothing at all on the research are building solar farms at prices very few people predicted just 10 years ago.[8] The Human Genome Project was funded mainly by the US government and carried out by 20 institutions in 6 countries. Its results were made public and now underpin medicine everywhere.[9] We can do the same thing for meat, with public investment in open-access research (GFI’s top priority worldwide). 

Eliminating the most egregious abuses is important, but it’s not enough.

One area where advocates are making progress is farm animal welfare. And make no mistake: If you were a hen in a cage or a mother pig in a crate, you would want advocates working hard to get you out. I am extremely supportive of this work, which earns a significant chunk of my personal philanthropy. 

But getting rid of the worst abuses (through welfare campaigns) and reducing the number of animals subjected to any abuse at all (through alternative proteins) accomplish different things. 

Welfare improvements are deeply meaningful, but even with them, conditions on industrial farms stay atrocious, both physically and mentally. These improvements matter so much precisely because conditions are the stuff of nightmares, whether for animals on land or in water. 

Welfare wins are also hard to scale globally. Most have come in the United States and the European Union, which account for about one-fifth of land animals slaughtered (17.3 of 87.9 billion) and just north of 1 percent of aquaculture (1.5 of 141 million metric tons).[10] Winning elsewhere is harder, and a victory in one country does not carry over to the next. 

So we need both: reducing the suffering of animals on farms now through welfare campaigns, and reducing the number of animals farmed through alternative meats that reach taste and price parity with conventional meat. Plant-based meat can substantially decrease the number of animals factory farmed, and cultivated meat has a real shot at cutting that number to zero, as I discuss here.

The Forum’s top two questions: Will it work, and will people eat it? 

Two questions about alternative meats recur most often on the EA Forum: Can plant-based and cultivated meat reach taste and price parity with conventional meat? And if they do, will people eat them? My first two Meat Matters articles tackle these questions. Here are the short versions: 

Scientific viability: More than 100 companies and hundreds of university scientists around the world are working to get cultivated meat to taste and price parity; those numbers are up from one (Upside Foods) and two (Mark Post and Marianne Ellis) just 11 years ago. At that point, Upside had raised just $125,000, which was all the private funding cultivated meat had ever received. Since then, costs have fallen by orders of magnitude, government funding and scientific progress have surged, and cultivated meat has gone from a $330,000 burger to full meals served to hundreds of people. I talk about why that's all quite mind-blowing in my first Meat Matters post. 

This feels a lot like solar and EVs a decade ago, when solar reached one percent of global electricity generation and EVs reached one percent of new car sales. For some cultivated meat companies, the central challenges now are regulatory approvals and securing the financing required to scale production. Those challenges are substantial, and success is far from certain, but the progress is deeply encouraging.[11]

Consumer acceptance: Consumer research suggests substantial interest in plant-based and cultivated meat, with good reason to expect that interest to grow further once products compete on taste and price (no product comes close right now).[12] At that point, benefits for food safety, the environment, global health, and animals can become additional reasons to choose them. On top of that, the economic and food security benefits give the meat industry and governments strong incentives to send price- and taste-competitive alt meats shooting up the adoption S-curve. I develop this argument here.

Will AGI or TAI solve cultivated meat? Let's make it happen! 

Some effective altruists expect artificial general intelligence (AGI) or transformative AI (TAI) to solve the taste and price challenges for alternative meats, and so they wonder: What's the point of work on alternative meats now? 

I’d love for that to happen, but I see at least three problems with waiting for it.

First, I’m not at all sure it’s true, absent significant effort from those of us who want to ensure that it happens. And as Lewis Bollard explained to Dwarkesh Patel, AI will also accelerate industrial animal farming. Unsurprisingly, AI is already making factory farming more efficient, and cheaper conventional meat makes competing on price harder.

Second, work we do now can make alternative proteins easier to advance with AI. We need much better data before machine learning can be maximally useful, we need trained scientists, and we need functioning companies. And then technical breakthroughs still have to become products: Facilities need financing, production needs scaling, and products need regulatory approval. They also need political support and the public’s trust. All of that requires an ecosystem, and that requires work right now. 

Third, speed matters. Every month, more than 18 billion vertebrate animals are farmed and slaughtered, each capable of feeling pain in much the same way we do. Animal scientist (and slaughterhouse designer) Temple Grandin has argued that they feel fear much more intensely than we do; in many cases, it’s incapacitatingly bad. And bioethicist Bernard Rollin has argued that pain may be worse for non-human animals, because they don’t know that it will end; in the moment, their suffering is their entire world.

My AI dream: a frontier lab takes on cultivated meat

Rather than wait for AGI to make meat without animals, let’s ask the people building it to help now. The science and engineering have advanced far enough that I think a frontier lab (e.g., the life sciences teams at Anthropic or OpenAI, or Google DeepMind) could solve the core challenges of making cultivated meat affordable, as I discuss here (and in much more depth in Meat). 

With their budgets, expertise, and connections, they could build the science and engineering roadmap for cheap cultivated meat and hand it to the world. With a bit more investment, they could speed up today’s startups or launch new ones, creating a thriving cultivated meat industry.

Most of the labs’ life sciences work focuses on medicine, and that work matters. But cultivated meat is a biology problem too, and solving it would end more suffering than almost anything else they could take on: hundreds of billions of vertebrate animals a year. 

And think about how cool it would be to change the very nature of nature by removing the need for live animals as a precursor to the production of animal meat.[13]

If you’re at a frontier lab and want to talk about making this happen, please get in touch. 

There is no plan B for reducing farm animal numbers, so let’s go all-in on alternative proteins.

If alternative meats fail, trillions more vertebrate animals will live miserable lives and die painful, terrifying deaths. Even if success were inevitable eventually (and I don't think it is), speed is a moral imperative: Every second, the world slaughters 2,800 land animals and 4,100 farmed finfish.

I believe that cultivated meat could eventually replace all industrial animal meat. But we don’t have to get anywhere near that goal to make an enormous difference. Displacing even 1 percent of conventional meat production means 2.2 billion fewer vertebrate animals each year living and dying in misery. 

I think a lot about the history of science and engineering, and how much progress has depended on hundreds of people each making specific choices at specific moments. In retrospect, breakthroughs can look inevitable. But behind them are people who chose to work on a difficult problem, fund an uncertain idea, or champion a technology before its promise was obvious.

In 2015, the International Energy Agency expected electric vehicles to remain a small share of the global car fleet through at least 2040. Why? In the IEA’s words, “the cost of batteries, consumer caution and limited recharging infrastructure.” Yet in 2025, electric cars made up 25 percent of new car sales worldwide and almost 55 percent in China, up from less than 1 percent a decade earlier.

How did that happen? Government policies in Europe, China, and the United States drove down battery costs, improved range, and paid for charging networks. Since 2015, battery prices have fallen about 75 percent, typical range has more than tripled, and the world has built more than 7 million public chargers. And companies, starting with Tesla, built cars good enough to shatter stereotypes about EVs and the people who drive them.

In each case, hundreds of people (or more) took actions they easily could have skipped, and history would have turned out worse. And in the version of history where they failed, everyone would simply assume the naysayers had been right: that these breakthroughs were never possible.

item.title: 80,000 Hours’ Shift To AI Is A Deep Loss For EA
item.description:
Published on October 27, 2026 5:10 PM GMT

Edit: Some people have pointed out that this post fails to make an argument for why AI shouldn't be 80,000 Hours' core focus, and I think that's a fair criticism. I don't want people who are concerned about AI to think I'm dismissing their concerns. At this time, I'm still quite uncertain about the topic so I don't feel committed to the view that AI takeover is likely. This post is more about processing my frustration about losing a meta-EA org.

This is a crosspost from my blog.

For as long as “effective altruism” has been a term, 80,000 Hours has been one its most important organizations - introducing new people to EA’s core ideas and helping them to find impactful careers.

Since March 2025, this has no longer been the case. This is because 80,000 Hours now primarily focuses on funneling people into careers in AI with the assumption that humanity is on the verge of AGI, which they believe could determine humanity’s future, possibly by bringing about either utopia or apocalypse.

I think this is a deep loss for EA, and I wanted to share some reasons why:

1. There’s no longer a good resource to introduce people to EA.

80,000 Hours’ career guide and its problem profiles used to be the very best resource for introducing people to the core ideas behind EA and motivating them to pursue impactful careers.

Now that it has an AGI worldview baked into its content, it no longer really fulfills that purpose since it’s about AI rather than EA.

This is quite sad to me given that, for a long time, 80,000 Hours was my favorite website, and I used to mention it to people quite often.

Now, I feel quite uncomfortable sharing it with people.

For those looking for alternative resources, Probably Good is an EA career advice site that’s similar to how 80,000 Hours used to be, although it has a lot less content.

The Intro to EA page is also quite good.

2. EA should be about diversity of thought

Since EA is about finding the most effective ways to do good, I think that diversity of thought is paramount to its success as a project. This is because you really can only expand and refine your worldview in a responsible way when you engage with people who disagree with you or offer different perspectives.

Given that 80,000 Hours puts the imminence of AGI as the background assumption to its content, it cuts off virtually all other worldviews about what “doing the most good” should look like.

In the worst case scenario, if 80,000 Hours turns EA into just another AI worldview, that strips EA of its fundamental value as “the science of doing good.”

3. Less people are discovering EA now.

According to the EA Survey 2024, 80,000 Hours was the second most common way that people learned about EA.

Since 80,000 Hours now focuses on funneling people into AI safety rather than EA, the EA movement will need to find new ways to gain attention.

4. 80,000 Hours’ content is increasingly bizarre, which is bad for EA.

80,000 Hours’ problem profiles page has 14 cause areas highlighted.

Of these, roughly eight are very esoteric and strange. (“Extreme power concentration [from AI],” “Engineered pandemics,” “Moral status of digital minds,” “Gradual disempowerment,” “S-risks,” “AI-enhanced decision making,” “Space governance,” and “Wild animal suffering”).

item.description:
Published on October 28, 2026 6:55 AM GMT

With the AI windfall, mental health may be taken increasingly seriously by mainstream EA. There’s increasingly room to explore the cause area and answer some of the biggest uncertainties; at the same time, costs of the most effective interventions are continuing to fall. StrongMinds is now treating for ~$35, about a third of GiveWell’s best guess from a few years ago, and is expected to fall further.

This presents a unique opportunity to demonstrate that mental health interventions should be considered as part of broader global health portfolios. We can do so by making methodological improvements to our cost-effectiveness analyses.

The Happier Lives Institute have pioneered (and are constantly improving) methods for CEAs of mental health in WELLBY terms. However, their mission doesn’t cover other forms of outcomes, such as DALYs and income doublings. Furthermore, they haven’t yet publicly explored models of psychotherapy that leave lasting impacts on individuals (which may be of interest to HLI). Therefore, with an eye to increasing the estimated impact of mental health interventions in ways that are legible to mainstream EAs, I propose three directions for EA-flavoured mental health research.

About me: I’m Huw, I work at Kaya Guides, an EA mental health charity[1]. This is based on my own experience of building our CEA, and reviewing other people’s CEAs of us. As such, I only consider CEAs for psychotherapy—other interventions are much more neglected and they would also be promising, but I have no expertise in these areas. I don’t have formal psychotherapy training or research experience; I only have a degree in statistics. As such, I am likely missing important facts and many of my estimates may not be high quality.

Converting symptom severity to DALYs

Due to HLI’s excellent focus on the WELLBY, combined with CG/GiveWell’s neglect of mental health, there hasn’t been a lot of work in writing DALY conversions. Prior art is:

  • SoGive: Their CEA of StrongMinds has a unique methodology, which you can read more on in their post. I won’t discuss this in depth, but the methodology isn’t standardised or adapted from something else, so my fear is that it’s too speculative to be trusted more widely.
  • Founders Pledge: They developed a method which takes GBD weights and interpolates them between PHQ-9 states, for their StrongMinds CEA. However, Founders Pledge have since moved to using WELLBYs for mental health CEAs. This CEA is also rather rough.
  • UK Green Book: Converts WELLBYs to DALYs at a naïve ratio of 7:1. (See page 55 in Wellbeing Guidance for Appraisal). Non-EA.
  • Furukawa et al. 2021: Used a mapping dataset to convert PHQ-9 scores to EQ-5D scores, which are the basis of QALYs. We can then naïvely convert QALYs 1:1 to DALYs, although there is little precedent here in EA, to my knowledge. A nice feature of this dataset is that it has different scales for PHQ-9 scores at pre- and post-, to represent the importance of expectations of treatment in quality of life.

I’d like to focus on the Founders Pledge approach, because the Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD) is the generally-accepted source for DALYs within EA. A DALY in EA is calculated by multiplying out the GBD’s disability weight for a condition, by the length of time under which that condition is averted.

As such, if we could determine a single, ‘canonical’ way of estimating the disability weights produced by an intervention, we could get to DALYs very quickly. The challenge with disability weights today is that they are determined under the GBD by asking global survey respondents which of two described health conditions is ‘healthier’. For depression, respondents are given three descriptions:

  • Mild: Feels persistent sadness and has lost interest in usual activities. Sometimes sleeps badly, feels tired, or has trouble concentrating, but still manages to function in daily life with extra effort.
  • Moderate: Has constant sadness and has lost interest in usual activities. Has some difficulty in daily life, sleeps badly, has trouble concentrating, and sometimes thinks about harming themselves.
  • Severe: Has overwhelming, constant sadness and cannot function in daily life. Sometimes loses touch with reality and wants to harm or kill themselves.

The GBD then does some fancy statistical fitting to determine a weight (0–1) for each condition. Mild is 0.145, moderate is 0.396, and severe is 0.658. We also know from Salomon et al. 2015 that the weights are fit in logit-space, so we can reasonably interpolate between them.

However, we have no ability to assign PHQ-9 scores to this scale confidently—PHQ-9 scores weren’t used anywhere in the construction of the GBD. Existing approaches have assumed some kind of linear interpretation, but we must be careful about assuming that a GBD ‘mild’ is the same thing as a PHQ-9 ‘mild’ (to say nothing of the PHQ-9s ‘moderately severe’).

Converting SF-12 scores

One method that hews closely to the GBD would be to assess SF-12 scores. This is because the GBD’s statistical estimates work by comparing the survey preferences to a dataset of SF-12 scores for the same conditions. In Burnstein et al. 2015, the authors map SF-12 scores to GBD weights, and then assess different conditions in terms of SF-12 scores (as well as using third-party datasets for the same).

If we had a useful dataset for mapping PHQ-9s to SF-12s, then we could convert those through to GBD weights by either recreating Burnstein’s mapping function, or by asking Burnstein to produce their function directly.

I was able to identify two usable studies for this purpose:

  • The MEPS panel survey: This study from the U.S. includes paired PHQ-2 and SF-12 summaries. As the PHQ-2 is a subset of the PHQ-9, we can then map to SF-12s. This dataset was also usable by AI to replicate Burnstein’s SF-12 to disability weight mapping function. I don’t have enough confidence in the results here to include them here.
  • Yu et al. 2012: This asked PHQ-9s and SF-12s for 6,000+ people with depression in Hong Kong. My AI was able to use their summaries to produce a mapping between the two; one could also see if they still have the raw dataset.

However, I think this direction is less likely to be useful because (a) the two datasets we have aren’t representative of LMIC populations and (b) it involves an extra conversion step, for which we’re likely to see some loss. The PHQ-2 is particularly suspect, because although it’s useful as a diagnostic tool, people who are merely sad will score highly on it but not be generally depressed—this would potentially underestimate the disability weight of saturating the scale, relative to a depressed population.

Directly mapping PHQ-9s to disability weights

Another direction to explore is how to directly map PHQ-9s to disability weights. One way of doing this is for a researcher to subjectively decide how the three GBD bands correspond to PHQ-9 scores, using their intuition. This is how existing approaches have functioned. However, the choices of bands and mappings here impact the resulting DALY estimates quite meaningfully. It’s my opinion that a small amount of work to standardise this method could pay off fairly substantially.

Another somewhat more objective way would be to use a survey. Respondents could adopt a ‘persona’ as one of the three (+neutral) states, and then fill in a PHQ-9 survey as that person. Respondents could be human, or potentially AI. We could then fit a reasonable mapping between the scores.

The final option is to find populations of depressed people, have them fill in a PHQ-9, and then ask a single vignette:

One last question. Here are three people. Thinking about the past 2 weeks, which person is most like you?

  • Person A: Enjoys usual activities and time with others. Sometimes feels sad or low for a day or two when something goes wrong, but it passes. Sleeps, concentrates, and manages daily life as usual.
  • Person B: Feels persistent sadness and has lost interest in usual activities. Sometimes sleeps badly, feels tired, or has trouble concentrating, but still manages to function in daily life with extra effort.
  • Person C: Has constant sadness and has lost interest in usual activities. Has some difficulty in daily life, sleeps badly, has trouble concentrating, and sometimes thinks about harming themselves.
  • Person D: Has overwhelming, constant sadness and cannot function in daily life. Sometimes loses touch with reality and wants to harm or kill themselves.

I’ve invented Person A’s description as the inverse of the others, while the others are taken from the GBD (I believe a ‘none of these’ option would be too confusing). We could then fit a curve on these.

Because the EA mental health space is fairly well-connected, a coordinated effort here between organisations could produce fairly large datasets for this question across the global south—we could partner with charities in India, Ecuador, South Africa, Kenya, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Uganda, the Phillipines, and so on. Kaya Guides will be asking this question ourselves and I expect to put together a dataset soon (reach out if you’d like to partner on this!).

Understanding long-term effects of psychotherapy

Cuijpers et al. 2026 is an important meta-analysis, which was unable to rule out the hypothesis that depression’s effects may last indefinitely. If this is true, then existing EA CEAs may be dramatically underestimating the impact of psychotherapy, potentially by a factor of 2–15x. However, there isn’t enough existing evidence that can be used to estimate this.

If this were true, CEAs could also start to access the value of suicide prevention, since we could argue that psychotherapy permanently averts suicides, rather than merely postponing them. (In my own BOTECs, suicide prevention wouldn’t provide a meaningful part of a CEA today, because of how rare suicide is, combined with the assumption that suicide prevention only lasts until the next episode of depression).

In my opinion, we should model depression as an episodic disorder. If this is true, then a course of psychotherapy may shorten, or lessen the severity of, an existing episode of depression. Under the GBD’s own analysis (Appendix 1), the mean episode of depression lasts around 0.65 years. This means that by the time of 12-month follow-up, most study participants would have completed the episode they started the study with, in both arms. As such, 12-month follow-ups are only catching (1) participants in the midst of very long episodes or (2) participants who have begun a subsequent episode.

Such a study is then almost certainly underpowered to detect effects (if it were powered for post-treatment), as only ~10% of the study population would be in an episode at 12 months (according to a BOTEC I did to simulate a bunch of episodes). The same can be said for later follow-ups. It’s very rare that large enough studies are conducted to detect effects under this measurement paradigm—but this could be a direction for future research.

Another direction could be to develop or standardise methods for determining long-term effects. Under an episodic model, we would need to capture a longitudinal sense of the participant’s trajectory. We could do this in two ways:

  1. Periodic sampling: Every month, send a questionnaire to participants, over many years. We could then calculate the area under the curve.
    1. This method is likely to be very challenging, due to attrition. You would immediately run into sampling bias, as only dedicated people would fill in the survey. It would be expensive, if incentives were to be offered.
    2. An alternative to this method would be to find a source of data that is already measuring the desired outcome periodically, such as a mood tracking app. You could partner with this app, and encourage participants in your intervention to use it (or you could make your own intervention useful after the treatment term).
  2. Retrospective interviewing: There are two main precedents here, but neither is widely used. The first is the LIFE interview, and the second is the NIMH Life Chart.
    1. Measurement will be hard and expensive if using humans for the interviews. However, a team could convert one of these into a structured questionnaire, or use recent advances in AI to piece together the life chart.
    2. The methods don’t have to be particularly accurate to find an effect with reasonable enough statistical power. Some modelling could be done here to determine precise sample sizes under different assumptions of recall.
    3. Such a method could be paired with a more expensive or biased periodic sampling method, to validate its accuracy.

I suspect this is a good research direction for a funded academic study, although perhaps some easy wins could be taken with basic research.

Economic impacts of psychotherapy

Some studies of the economic impacts of depression put the value at a percentage of GDP. Given depression’s prevalence, this implies economic losses of ~20% of income—nothing to sneeze at. Meta-analyses of the effects of psychotherapy on labour-market outcomes find around ~0.15 standard deviations on most outcomes.

More work needs to be done to establish the precise effect sizes, and then convert these to income doublings, to be taken seriously by CG. Similarly, more work needs to be done in establishing appropriate discounts and methodologies for including these effect sizes in CEAs. Many outcomes simply don’t show up as statistically significant.

Similarly, another concern worth researching is that causal impacts of psychotherapy don’t seem to recover a proportionate amount of the burden of depression on GDP. It would be worth understanding why this is, and doing more work to quantify the effects.

Much of the work in this field has involved Johannes Haushofer, who Kaya Guides is collaborating with on our RCT. In the next few weeks, we’ll start our RCT with a very large sample size (around 3,500 participants), which by our count will be one of the largest ever studies of any psychosocial intervention in South Asia. The hope is that at these sample sizes, we’d be able to find effects on measures that other studies have struggled with (such as income at 12 months).

Conclusion

Overall, however, an impact of 0.15sd seems unlikely to move the needle. Improving PHQ-9/DALY conversions improves the credibility and legibility of mental health CEAs for relatively cheap, and studying the long-term effects of mental health interventions could yield substantially larger effects than previously estimated. So economic impacts seem like the least promising direction.

As well as work to improve mental health CEAs, organisations in the space need to communicate better about what has changed since GiveWell’s CEA of StrongMinds. Kaya Guides are guilty of this ourselves, and I’m hoping to share more on this soon.

If you’re interested in pursuing any of these research questions further, please reach out to me!

item.title: Keeping the EA Forum alive
item.description:
Published on October 28, 2026 4:03 PM GMT

I’m a bit concerned that the EA Forum is going to die a slow death. I don’t want this to happen as it has long been, in my opinion, the best place on the internet. I'd like it to stay that way. I personally have found myself engaging less, because the content is less interesting and relevant to me.

I also think some of the trends I highlight below are due to CEA investing less in the Forum (e.g., my impression is the Forum team is smaller than it used to be). I think a lot of what I critique below is downstream of community dynamics, rather than the Forum itself. But I also think injecting the EA Forum with a vibrant intellectual culture will be good for EA as a whole.

The point of this post is to open a discussion, and give my own ideas for what I think might help. I welcome people to disagree, share their own takes on what the EA Forum should be, and the purpose it serves.

EA Forum moderators — I think you all do an admirable job. My personal view is that there should be way more of you doing way more to keep the community vibrant. To the extent this is a critique of your work, it's coming from a place of thinking that you are doing an essential community service that I want more of.

It's possible that the death of the EA Forum is downstream from other community dynamics (like a massive shift to AI safety from previously highly engaged people). But the EA Forum could have been (and maybe still could be) a place where these ideas were discussed. My guess is that a strong EA Forum is actually a fundamental part of keeping EA thriving, as long as EA is going to be a global movement, and working actively to keep it strong is essential to the future of EA.

Is the EA Forum dying?

I think so. Here's 10 years of data on EA Forum engagement:

My interpretation of these data is that the number of users and top-level posts on the Forum has steadily increased, with a massive spike then decline around FTX, but otherwise the Forum just continues to grow. But until the post-FTX decline, other important metrics, like comments from high-karma users, highly-upvoted posts, and comments generally were also increasing. Post-FTX, these metrics have all declined precipitously. Comments per post, which I think is the most important EA Forum success metric (if we want to Goodhart anything), have declined across this entire period. I think this is especially bad — it means that more and more, the Forum is being filled with posts that readers don't find to be worth talking about!

I think the ideal version of the Forum is fewer, higher quality posts, and way more comments. Ideally, those comments are from highly engaged people, who are having useful discourse about disagreements and cruxes. These trends suggest the opposite: there are more posts from more people, but these posts aren't heavily engaged with (suggesting that they don't say anything useful?), and aren't engaged with by the highest context people.

What’s the value of the Forum?

I used to think the EA Forum was mainly fun and distracting, and didn't think it was that valuable. But I've realized in seeing it decline that it was actually core to EA succeeding as an intellectual movement, and meaningfully increased the quality of the community. I was wrong about it being a distraction — it was serving some important functions:

  • It was a central conversation ground for the EA community.
  • It provided a good way to disseminate information to EAs / share research that might be relevant to people.
  • It was a place where you can be somewhat certain that ~most highly engaged EAs will see at least the title of your post, if not read it.
  • It kept globally dispersed people engaged with the ideas of EA, and kept active intellectual discourse alive.

Currently, I think the weight is shifting:

  • There isn't really a central conversation place for EAs — discussion seems to happen in disjointed private events, at EA Globals, or on Substack (though I think the discussion quality on Substack is much worse, even though many posts are good).
  • I don't think many professional EAs read the Forum regularly anymore.
  • The Forum seems to have a lot more people who are new to EA, and it is filled with content that seems to rehash old discussions, which doesn't get much engagement.

To me, the EA Forum was the core intellectual center of EA in the past. It was a place where there was reliably extremely high-quality discussion about difficult ideas. I think that the best version of EA maintains this, and getting the Forum to that place again is pretty important for the future of EA.

Ideas for saving the Forum

A lot of my thinking here is informed by LessWrong. I typically don't find LessWrong content as relevant to me as good EA Forum content, but LessWrong seems to have been much more successful at keeping their intellectual culture alive. It has much heavier moderation than the EA Forum, and they create bigger walls around new users posting. I think this post in particular highlights a philosophy that has kept LessWrong successful while the Forum has declined.

Here are a bunch of ideas that I think would help the Forum do a better job at keeping its own culture alive.

  • Stop the posting of Substack slop.
    • Substack pushes people to post a lot, which is good for their bottom line. But posting a lot drives down quality, because authors feel like they have to put something up even when they don't have much to say. As a result, most posts on Substack are worse than a good EA Forum piece, and authors cross-posting to the Forum are porting that bad outcome here.
      • I'm am one of the people guilty of this. Many of these authors are great researchers or thinkers who have written thoughtful things in the past. They should save those pieces for the Forum, and stop using the Forum as a way to generate subscriptions on Substack. I might be in favor of fully moderated cross-posts just to prevent this.
    • Note that Substack posts often are good and contain good ideas! I am calling them slop here because they don't really advance the conversations that are essential to EA, aren't interesting to discuss, and just flood the Forum with boring and obvious points in order to get Anthropic donors' eyes on them, or to generate subscriptions.
    • Examples of Substack posts I don't consider to meet the bar I want to hold the EA Forum to (including my own because I'm naming names):
      • My own on starting nonprofits quickly
      • Partially-AI generated content exclusively for lab donors
      • Partially-AI generated content mostly for lab donors
      • People advertising their Substacks
      • More Substack advertising
    • I've purposely selected authors who regularly write content far above the bar for the Forum, to illustrate that it is not author quality that causes this dynamic, but post-frequency pressures or a cultural shift or something else. Substack rewards posting all the time, but the EA Forum shouldn't — it should reward posting really good stuff.
  • Relatedly, we don't need a marginal millionth piece on how Anthropic donors should engage with philanthropic advisors or think about their giving.
  • Generally discourage cross-posting
    • I think that cross-posted things are sometimes useful, but I've noticed that most cross-posted things get little engagement, and just bury the Forum in less relevant content. Maybe the Forum should have a sidebar where people can submit relevant links that are voted on or commented on (more like Hacker News) that aren't primary posts? This could also help with the Substack slop issue — those posts can go there, and be voted on based on relevance.
  • Generally don't post links to the EA Forum on Substack (to prevent random people from engaging without an understanding of the context).
    • People shouldn't do this stuff — it just causes brigading / increases in low-quality accounts and comments. Advertising this post on Substack does nothing for the EA community, and degrades the quality of the Forum.
    • Obviously there are times where linking to the Forum is useful, and this is mainly a cultural norm, not something the Forum team can enforce. But I think a stronger norm of being thoughtful about audiences on the Forum versus elsewhere would be good.
  • Rate limit new posters until the acquire some amount of karma via comments.
    • I think part of what makes the Forum great is that the people you engage with are good faith, say thoughtful things, and have a high degree of reasoning transparency. People are rewarded for doing this well via karma and upvotes. I think it is fine to rate-limit people who do this poorly, or haven't yet demonstrated that they can do this (e.g., new users) until they reach certain karma thresholds.
    • LessWrong has better policies on this, and the EA Forum should do the same.
  • Heavily down-weight or ban AI-generated content
    • I think LessWrong's relatively strict LLM policing is much better than the Forum's. As time goes on, the Forum has gotten more low-quality AI-generated posts. They get labelled as such, but are still bad. Forcing that content into separate, labelled blocks within posts, and moderating out violations seems good for keeping the Forum high quality.
  • Do more prizes, contests, and events.
    • I think that running things like the EA Forum prizes, contests, and other events usually significantly improve post quality. The Forum could go back to doing way more of this!
  • Addressing my personal pet peeve: let users choose how their content is licensed.
    • Currently, all content posted on the EA Forum is licensed under a CC-BY license. That means it can be used commercially by anyone as long as there is attribution. I am free to, for example, sell and profit off a book that takes your posts and repackages them without your permission, as long as I attribute the authorship to you.
    • I generally like Creative Commons licenses, but this specifically does cause me to post fewer things on the Forum, because I sometimes don't want to give people that ability! If this is true for other people, I think that either authors choosing their own license, or changing the default to CC-BY Non-Commercial would be better.
    • Additionally, in past roles, this sometimes led to issues (e.g. if a contract funds me to write something, and the contract-holder owns the copyright, even if they are okay with me sharing the post, they might not want me to allow it to be used by others commercially). LessWrong just allows users to own their posted work and license it how they please, which seems much cleaner.

One of the most obvious objections to what I'm saying here is that it is creating a gate-kept version of EA where newcomers don't have any way to get involved. But I think the EA Forum should not be a tool for community growth, and therefore shouldn't be optimized for that purpose. There need to be places for people new to EA to learn and talk about these ideas, but I think it is okay for the Forum to not be that, and instead be a place where highly-engaged people can push these ideas forward.

  • I think the Forum works best when everyone has some baseline of shared knowledge, context, and vocabulary. That means it shouldn't be a place where people brand new to EA share their ideas without historic context on how they've been discussed.
  • The EA community has tons of introductory reading materials, fellowships, and ways for newcomers to get involved. The Forum should cater to insiders and more heavily engaged people. Things like the Featured page push the other direction.
  • If this is right, there are a variety of adjustments that could be made to prioritize discussion between relative experts, rather than introductory content.
    • Make the Forum invite only — give existing users, maybe based on karma, the ability to invite new people, and don't let people freely register (you can also give fellowship organizers, student organizers, core organizations, etc. the ability to invite people freely, to ensure there are a diversity of pathways in).
    • Have people apply to get accounts, and discuss their engagement with EA in that application.
    • If the Forum doesn't make registration invite-only, I think it could consider having introductory sequences for people to read through when they register. Often, new users will post ideas that have been discussed extensively before, and would benefit from seeing big hits and discussion from the past before posting.

A second objection might be that more content is better, and more content drives engagement more than quality. For example, Seth Ariel Green recently called for a lower bar to posting, because they feel that their community is letting the perfect be the enemy of the good.

The question is, what is growth and engagement for? If community building, see above. But if idea generating and refining, then I disagree -- high quality posts do this a lot better than high volume. I don't think that should mean a strong conceptual piece sits in drafts for ever because it's not stylistically polished. But I do mean: post when you have something interesting and important to say, and you've thought about it a lot!
